units.title: Introduction to software architecture
units.description: Explain architectural decisions, compare intended and implemented structures, and choose views and patterns for a system.

chapters.title: Why software needs architecture
paragraphs: Software supports everyday activities, and a large system can exceed what any one developer can understand at once. The historical codebase examples in the slides illustrate growth and complexity. Their exact line counts are snapshots, not a measure of design quality or a rule for when architecture becomes necessary.

Complexity creates practical questions: where should a change go, what might it break, how can we inspect security and quality, and how will the system run and evolve? Architecture provides a manageable account of important parts, their relationships, and the decisions that constrain them. It connects a problem and its requirements to a solution that developers can implement and test.

The engineering analogy in the slides emphasizes planning, coordination, and checking the result. It does not require every decision to be completed before coding. Architectural reasoning can continue as implementation and feedback reveal new constraints. Maintenance and evolution make preserving the reasons behind important decisions valuable.
chapters.prediction: Two systems have the same number of source lines. Must they need the same architectural effort?
chapters.explanation: No. Relationships, stakeholder concerns, quality requirements, and the cost of changing important decisions matter. Line count alone does not reveal these factors.
chapters.narration: Software architecture helps us reason about a system that is too complex to hold entirely in our heads. The slides use growing codebases to motivate this problem. Architecture connects requirements to important structural decisions, and helps people locate changes, examine quality, and plan evolution. Size alone does not determine the effort required. Ask which decisions affect many parts of the system, and which assumptions would be expensive to change.
chapters.focus: Connect complexity, requirements, and decisions.

chapters.title: Systems, stakeholders, and decisions
paragraphs: A system exists in an environment and serves a mission. Its stakeholders are people or organizations with an interest in its behavior or development. For a museum catalog, the mission might be to help visitors discover exhibits; curators, visitors, and maintainers have different concerns. State the system boundary so that external people and systems are not mistaken for internal components.

The definitions in the slides emphasize components, relationships, interfaces, behavior, composition, and guiding principles. Architectural decisions are the design decisions significant to the system as a whole: they shape how major responsibilities fit together and how important qualities can be achieved. Architecture is design, but a local design choice is not automatically architecturally significant.

Significance depends on context. An algorithm or data structure can become an architectural concern if it determines system-wide performance, compatibility, or feasible behavior. Conversely, a small local implementation choice may be easy to replace. Architecture supports communication among stakeholders, analysis of a proposed system, and reuse of successful structures; a diagram is useful only when people agree on its meaning.
chapters.prediction: Is choosing an algorithm always outside software architecture?
chapters.explanation: No. A locally replaceable algorithm may be detailed design, but one that constrains the whole system or determines a critical quality can be architecturally significant.
chapters.narration: Begin with the system mission, its environment, and its stakeholders. Then identify the decisions that strongly shape structure and behavior. Architecture includes important responsibilities, interfaces, relationships, and principles. Not every design choice has the same reach. Even an algorithm can be architectural when it determines a system-wide quality. The purpose is to support communication and analysis, so a useful description explains why its decisions matter to the people involved.
chapters.focus: Judge a decision by its consequences, not its label.

chapters.title: Intended and implemented architecture
paragraphs: Prescriptive, or intended, architecture describes how the system is supposed to be organized. Descriptive, or implemented, architecture describes what actually exists. The two can differ because software evolves, documentation becomes stale, or implementation decisions bypass agreed boundaries. Treat an intended diagram as a statement of design intent, not proof of the current code structure.

Architecture drift means new implementation decisions are absent from the intended description without violating it. Architecture erosion means the implementation violates the intended architecture. Suppose the intended design permits a presentation module to call only an application interface. An allowed new implementation behind that interface may be undocumented drift; a direct presentation-to-storage dependency violates the stated boundary and is erosion.

Architecture recovery reconstructs an account of the implemented system from evidence such as source code, executable structure, configuration, and developer knowledge. Record uncertainty rather than filling gaps with guesses. Compare the recovered account with the intended one, investigate differences, and decide whether to repair the implementation or deliberately revise the intended design and its rationale.
chapters.prediction: An undocumented component is added within all permitted dependency rules. Is that necessarily erosion?
chapters.explanation: No. Under the distinction in the slides, a compatible undocumented decision is drift. Erosion requires evidence of a violated intended rule.
chapters.narration: An intended architecture states how a system should be organized. An implemented architecture describes what exists. Drift adds undocumented decisions without violating the intended design; erosion breaks an intended constraint. To distinguish them, first identify the actual rule, then inspect evidence of the implementation. Architecture recovery helps reconstruct that evidence. A team can repair a violation or consciously revise a decision, but should keep its description and rationale aligned with the result.
chapters.focus: Distinguish missing documentation from violated constraints.

chapters.title: Views and meaningful diagrams
paragraphs: A single box-and-arrow picture rarely answers every architectural question. A static decomposition can show code responsibilities and dependencies. A runtime view can show processes and interactions. A deployment view can show where software executes across devices. State what each box and arrow represents, and distinguish a code dependency from a runtime message or a deployment relationship.

The 4+1 model organizes complementary views. The logical view describes key abstractions and responsibilities; the process view addresses runtime concurrency and interactions; the development view describes code organization; the physical view maps software onto hardware or execution nodes. The additional scenarios connect and help examine the views through representative system behavior.

For a museum catalog, a logical view might distinguish exhibits and collections, a development view might show modules, and a physical view might place the application on a server. A visitor searching for an exhibit is a scenario that can be traced through the relevant views. These descriptions must agree, but they need not contain identical boxes or identical levels of detail.
chapters.prediction: A maintainer asks which device runs a process. Would a class diagram alone answer the question?
chapters.explanation: Usually not. A physical or deployment view identifies execution placement. A class diagram describes a different concern and needs an explicit mapping to runtime and deployment elements.
chapters.narration: A diagram needs a question and a legend. Boxes may represent domain concepts, modules, processes, or machines; arrows may mean very different things. The four plus one model separates logical, process, development, and physical concerns, and uses scenarios to connect them. Choose a view for the question being asked. Then check that the views agree about the same system, without trying to put every detail into one crowded picture.
chapters.focus: Choose a view and define its notation.

chapters.title: Abstraction, reuse, and C4
paragraphs: Architectural descriptions can reuse ideas at different scopes. A style describes a family of structures through constraints on elements and relationships. A reference architecture gives a reusable architectural organization for a domain. A product-line architecture captures shared structure and planned variation across related products. These concepts help teams reuse reasoning, rather than copy a diagram without checking its assumptions.

C4 provides four nested levels of structural description: system context, containers, components, and code. Context shows the system in relation to people and external systems. Containers show major running applications or data stores within the system; components describe responsibilities within a container; code shows implementation detail when useful. A C4 container is a modeling concept, not necessarily a Docker container.

C4 levels and 4+1 views answer different organizing questions. C4 changes the level of detail; 4+1 separates concerns such as code organization and runtime processes. Neither requires every diagram for every audience. Architectural significance also does not follow a fixed line-count threshold or a rule that architecture happens only early: revisit consequential decisions as the system evolves.
chapters.prediction: A context diagram contains every class in the application. Does the extra detail necessarily help its audience?
chapters.explanation: No. A context audience needs the system boundary, people, and external relationships. Class detail can obscure that purpose; move it to a more detailed description when it answers a relevant question.
chapters.narration: Reusable architectural ideas include styles, reference architectures, and product-line architectures. Their assumptions and constraints matter as much as their shapes. C4 offers nested descriptions: context, containers, components, and code. These levels help match detail to an audience. A container here means a running application or data store, not necessarily a packaging technology. C4 levels and four plus one views are complementary ways to organize descriptions, rather than interchangeable lists.
chapters.focus: Match abstraction to audience and purpose.

chapters.title: Patterns and architectural styles
paragraphs: An architectural pattern describes a recurring design problem and an arrangement of responsibilities that addresses it in a context. A style constrains the kinds of elements and relationships allowed in a family of architectures. The terms can overlap in use; explaining the responsibilities, constraints, and consequences is more useful than relying only on a name.

The three-tier example separates presentation, application processing, and data management. This helps identify responsibilities and the interfaces between them. A logical separation of these concerns does not by itself prove that they run on three separate machines. MVC separates model, view, and controller responsibilities around an interface; it should not be assumed to be a one-to-one synonym for three deployment tiers.

The sense–compute–control example organizes observation, computation, and action on an environment. It highlights a different set of responsibilities from a typical presentation-and-data application. When selecting any pattern, state the problem it addresses and the constraints it imposes. A named style may support desired qualities, but its name alone cannot guarantee maintainability, performance, or other outcomes.
chapters.prediction: A team labels three boxes MVC. Has it demonstrated a three-machine deployment?
chapters.explanation: No. MVC describes responsibilities. Deployment requires separate evidence about where those responsibilities execute; a diagram label does not establish placement.
chapters.narration: Patterns organize responsibilities around recurring problems. Three-tier architecture separates presentation, application processing, and data management. MVC focuses on model, view, and controller responsibilities, while sense, compute, control organizes observation and action. These are useful ideas, but labels do not establish deployment or guarantee quality. Explain the problem, the relationships, and the constraints. Then examine whether the proposed arrangement serves the system mission and stakeholder concerns.
chapters.focus: Explain responsibilities and constraints behind a pattern.

quiz.question: How does an architectural decision differ from an ordinary local design choice?
quiz.answer: Its significance comes from its system-wide consequences, relationships, quality concerns, or cost of change. The boundary is contextual, not a fixed size or phase rule.

quiz.question: What evidence distinguishes architecture drift from erosion?
quiz.answer: Compare the implemented decision with an explicit intended constraint. An undocumented compatible addition is drift; a violated constraint is erosion. Without a known constraint, do not assert a violation.

quiz.question: How do C4 levels differ from the 4+1 views?
quiz.answer: C4 organizes structural descriptions by abstraction level. The 4+1 model separates architectural concerns and relates them through scenarios. They are not a one-to-one mapping.

exercise.prompt: Design an introductory architecture description for a museum exhibit catalog. State its mission and two stakeholders. Draw a system-context diagram and one complementary view, with a legend. Describe one significant decision, then explain how you would check whether the implementation follows it.
exercise.answer: A possible mission is helping visitors find exhibits. Visitors need understandable search results; curators need a maintainable catalog. The context diagram shows people, the catalog boundary, and any explicitly assumed external system. A development view can show presentation, application, and data-access modules with arrows meaning permitted dependencies. Record a decision that presentation uses the application interface, then inspect code dependencies for direct storage access. Other decompositions are valid when their rationale and notation are clear.

units.title: Jeromy: architecture, resilience and customer value
units.description: Connect architectural decisions to quality attributes, trace an outage through recovery dependencies, and design graceful degradation around customer value.

chapters.title: Architecture is a set of consequential decisions
paragraphs: Jeromy frames architecture around decisions that are difficult to change and strongly affect a system’s quality attributes. A component diagram helps describe a system, but architectural reasoning also explains why its boundaries, dependencies, storage and recovery mechanisms were chosen.

Whether a choice is architectural depends on context. A language choice may deeply affect latency, maintainability or hiring for a long-lived system; for a disposable prototype its consequences may be smaller. Avoid declaring a technology universally architectural without identifying the quality impact and cost of reversal.

For a new campus alerting service, ask which decisions determine whether acknowledged alerts survive a crash, whether operators can diagnose a failure, and whether a new delivery channel can be added. These questions connect the opening lecture to later requirements, database, microservices and QODA units.
chapters.prediction: Is a language choice always an architectural decision?
chapters.explanation: Its importance depends on how strongly it affects relevant qualities and how costly it is to reverse in the particular system.
chapters.narration: Architecture includes consequential decisions, especially those that are difficult to reverse and strongly affect quality. A box diagram is useful, but ask why the boundaries and dependencies exist. For an alerting service, durable acknowledgments and a working recovery path may matter more than a fashionable component name. Always connect the decision to its context.
chapters.focus: Architecture is a set of consequential decisions. Read the explanation, predict the outcome, then apply it.

chapters.title: Start with the customer’s quality priorities
paragraphs: The lecture’s simplified observability pipeline ingests telemetry, persists it, processes and indexes it, and supports alerts and queries. Those functions depend on one another: an alert cannot be trustworthy if the relevant data was never ingested.

In the historical Datadog example, durability is central to customer trust. Availability priorities include preserving ingestion and monitoring before less urgent query behavior. Another important measure is ingestion-to-use latency, including the time until data can support an alert. This ordering belongs to that business context, not every application.

A quality requirement should state which user outcome it protects. For a campus safety system, preserving an accepted urgent alert and delivering it on time might outrank historical report generation. State what may be delayed, what may be dropped, and what must not be lost. Apply authorization and data-retention constraints as part of the design.
chapters.prediction: If a dashboard is unavailable but accepted data is durably retained, are availability and durability identical outcomes?
chapters.explanation: No. The service can retain data while failing to provide timely access or alerts. Measure both properties and explain the user consequences.
chapters.narration: Start with customer outcomes. The lecture’s observability pipeline must ingest data before it can alert on that data. Durable storage, service availability and ingestion-to-alert latency are different qualities. Preserving accepted data is valuable even when a dashboard is unavailable, but it does not make the outage harmless. Set priorities explicitly for the application.
chapters.focus: Start with the customer’s quality priorities. Read the explanation, predict the outcome, then apply it.

chapters.title: Trace a correlated failure across the system
paragraphs: Jeromy describes the March 2023 Datadog outage as a historical case study. An unattended operating-system update restarted networking software and disrupted routing on many nodes. A change outside the ordinary staged rollout path crossed otherwise separate deployment boundaries.

The lesson is about correlated causes. Multiple machines, regions or cloud providers do not guarantee independence when a shared update mechanism can affect them together. Include operating-system packages, configuration, identity, networking and management services in the dependency and change-control review.

Recovery behavior also differed across cloud environments in the case described. Replacing a machine and rebooting a machine can have different consequences for local state. Treat these as historical observations from the recording, not guarantees about current cloud-provider behavior. A recovery plan must specify what survives each action and how service state is reconstructed.
chapters.prediction: Can a geographically replicated system still have one broad failure mechanism?
chapters.explanation: Yes. A shared configuration, update, credential or control-plane dependency can fail across regions. Geographic diversity protects only against the failure classes it actually separates.
chapters.narration: The historical outage illustrates a correlated failure. A networking update affected many machines through a shared change mechanism. Replication did not isolate that cause. Recovery then differed across environments because replacing a node and rebooting it preserve different state. Review the entire control and update path, and document what each recovery action destroys or retains.
chapters.focus: Trace a correlated failure across the system. Read the explanation, predict the outcome, then apply it.

chapters.title: Durability, bootstrap dependencies and tested restoration
paragraphs: Multiple persistence stages helped preserve data in the case: client-side buffering, local journals and durable messaging provided different opportunities for recovery. Buffers still need capacity and a policy for sustained downstream failure. A persistent queue is not an infinite sink.

One protective circumstance was that many messaging nodes did not share the affected operating-system version. Jeromy explicitly cautions against treating delayed upgrades as the lesson. The useful questions concern failure-domain diversity, safe update procedures and tested recovery, not avoiding security maintenance.

Startup dependencies can form cycles even when normal operation seems healthy. If service A needs B to start and B needs A, restoring both from zero may require an independent bootstrap path. Identify such cycles in advance, document the minimal recovery set, and rehearse it.

A stored backup is not proof of recoverability. Test restoration into the environment that will exist after the failure, measure recovery time, and verify the resulting data. The case also contrasts independently recoverable shards with systems that need enough cooperating members before serving; actual behavior depends on the design and failure assumptions.
chapters.prediction: A team has daily backups but has never restored them. What is missing?
chapters.explanation: Evidence that the restore process works with available keys, dependencies, capacity and state. Rehearse restoration and validate the result and recovery time.
chapters.narration: Durability mechanisms matter only with a workable recovery path. Several persistence layers helped retain data, but queues have finite capacity. Backups need tested restores. Startup dependencies can form cycles that require a bootstrap mechanism. Rehearse a cold recovery so the first attempt is not under incident pressure. Do not mistake an accidental unupgraded component for a sound upgrade strategy.
chapters.focus: Durability, bootstrap dependencies and tested restoration. Read the explanation, predict the outcome, then apply it.

chapters.title: Recover customer value, not just machine count
paragraphs: A fleet can regain machines before customers regain useful service. Dependencies, backlog and competing work can make recovery uneven. The lecture emphasizes graceful degradation: as capacity falls, preserve the most valuable outcomes and relax lower-priority service where the requirements permit it.

Self-monitoring can also fail with the monitored system. Keep independent signals and operational access for diagnosing an outage. Manual procedures are useful only when practiced; a recovery runbook should identify its dependencies and how it is tested.

New teaching calculation: incoming work is 100 items/second, recovered capacity is 120, and a durable backlog contains 6,000 items. Only 20 items/second remain for old work, so ideal drainage takes 300 seconds. At capacity 100 the backlog does not drain. This fluid model omits retries, variation and downstream bottlenecks; real recovery needs measurement.

Define priority classes, throttle backfill, and avoid overwhelming control services during mass provisioning. Exercise capacity loss in a controlled game day and measure end-to-end customer outcomes. Do not assume a universal percentage of remaining capacity guarantees useful service.
chapters.prediction: After machines return, why might service recovery still be slow?
chapters.explanation: Live arrivals, retries and stored backlog compete for limited resources; some dependent services may still be unavailable. Measure useful completed operations and backlog drainage, not only node count.
chapters.narration: Recovery should restore customer value. A system with a backlog needs spare capacity beyond new arrivals. At one hundred arrivals per second and one hundred twenty completions per second, only twenty items per second drain old work. Prioritize urgent traffic and throttle backfill deliberately. Practice degraded operation and retain independent visibility when the main monitoring path fails.
chapters.focus: Recover customer value, not just machine count. Read the explanation, predict the outcome, then apply it.

chapters.title: Apply quality thinking to AI-assisted development
paragraphs: The recording ends with a discussion of AI-assisted software development. Its architectural connection is long-term maintainability: rapidly producing code does not by itself show that a team can understand, operate, secure or change the result.

Treat the lecture’s tool usage and industry predictions as a 2025 discussion rather than current adoption statistics. The durable question is whether the resulting software meets explicit quality scenarios. A disposable personal prototype and a long-lived production service have different consequences if no one understands the implementation.

New exercise: an AI-generated incident dashboard works for a demonstration. Before deploying it as a lasting service, specify authorization, safe handling of untrusted input, failure behavior, diagnostic visibility and changeability. Review the implementation, test the relevant scenarios, and assign ownership for maintenance. Generated output still requires engineering evidence.
chapters.prediction: A generated application works in a demo. What architectural questions remain?
chapters.explanation: Whether it remains correct, secure, diagnosable, operable and maintainable under the intended workloads, failures and future changes. A demo demonstrates only the behavior exercised.
chapters.narration: The final discussion connects AI-assisted development to quality. Generating code quickly does not prove that a team can maintain or operate it. For a lasting service, define security, reliability and change scenarios, inspect the implementation and collect evidence. A successful demo is one observation, not a complete architectural evaluation.
chapters.focus: Apply quality thinking to AI-assisted development. Read the explanation, predict the outcome, then apply it.

quiz.question: Why can many replicas fail together?
quiz.answer: They may share an update mechanism, control plane, dependency or configuration. Review correlated causes rather than counting replicas alone.

quiz.question: How does durability differ from timely recovery?
quiz.answer: Durability preserves accepted state; recovery also requires capacity, working dependencies and tested reconstruction. Stored work may remain unavailable or delayed.

quiz.question: What should a game day measure?
quiz.answer: Customer-visible outcomes, recovery time, data integrity, backlog behavior and the usability of diagnostic and manual recovery paths under stated failures.

exercise.prompt: Design a degraded-operation and restoration plan for a campus alerting pipeline. Identify three correlated dependencies, separate urgent delivery from historical reporting, and define a cold-start rehearsal with measurable success criteria.
exercise.answer: State acknowledgment and loss semantics, buffer limits, priority policies, bootstrap dependencies and independent monitoring. Measure useful alert delivery and backlog drainage, and verify restoration. Explain tradeoffs and the conditions under which the plan cannot meet its goals.

review.issue: The recording describes a historical outage and deployment-specific behavior.
review.correction: Do not generalize its provider observations into current guarantees or treat delayed updates as a recommended defense.

review.issue: AI tool preferences and adoption comments reflect the 2025 discussion.
review.correction: The unit retains the architectural questions about evidence, maintainability and quality; it does not repeat adoption figures as current facts.

units.title: UML, design principles & SOLID
units.description: Read class relationships, reason about contracts, and use cohesion, composition, and abstractions to support change.

chapters.title: Read and write class diagrams
paragraphs: A class diagram summarizes selected structural facts. Class boxes can show names, attributes and operations; visibility symbols communicate access, while inheritance and interface realization express different contracts. Associations describe relationships between instances, with multiplicity constraining how many may participate. The BankAccount and Student–Course examples connect these symbols to code so that notation supports an explanation rather than becoming a memorization exercise.

Read multiplicity from the relevant association end and distinguish capacity from actual participation. An array with thirty slots is not evidence that thirty courses are always assigned. Composition expresses strong ownership in the model, whereas an ordinary association need not imply a shared lifetime. Nested classes, dependencies and notes add detail when needed. Correct partial snippets before treating them as runnable implementations, and state conventions where the diagram omits information.
chapters.prediction: Does a Student containing a Course array of length thirty imply exactly thirty enrolled courses?
chapters.explanation: No. Storage capacity does not establish actual enrollment; multiplicity should express the intended domain constraint.
chapters.narration: Read a class diagram as a precise but selective model. Identify classes, access levels, operations and relationships, then interpret multiplicities in the domain. Use code examples to check the model, especially when a collection’s capacity differs from actual membership. Ownership, inheritance and interface contracts communicate different ideas, so choose the relationship that matches the intended behavior.
chapters.focus: Classes, visibility, inheritance, associations, multiplicity, ownership, interfaces and dependencies.

chapters.title: Patterns as reusable design knowledge
paragraphs: UML can be used selectively to resolve a design question rather than to document every implementation detail. The cited industry study illustrates different usage patterns, not a universal adoption rate for every team. A diagram earns its place by helping collaborators reason. Design patterns likewise provide reusable language for a problem, a solution structure and the consequences that accompany it.

A pattern is not a mechanical recipe. Its forces and tradeoffs must fit the system, language and expected changes. The architectural-doorway example makes this concrete: the layout responds to patterns of movement rather than to an abstract preference for doors in corners. Composition delegates behavior through collaborating objects, while inheritance commits to a subtype relationship and its contracts. Prefer the mechanism that expresses the relationship and controls the intended variation.
chapters.prediction: Should every recurring code fragment be replaced by a named design pattern?
chapters.explanation: No. Use a pattern when its problem and tradeoffs match; adding structure without a need can reduce clarity.
chapters.narration: Patterns preserve design knowledge by naming recurring problems and explaining solutions and consequences. Apply them with judgment, not mechanically. Selective diagrams can help communicate the relevant structure. When comparing composition and inheritance, examine the relationship and the behavior clients depend on; reuse alone is not enough to justify a subtype hierarchy.
chapters.focus: Realistic UML usage, pattern structure and consequences, composition versus inheritance.

chapters.title: Single responsibility and cohesion
paragraphs: The single responsibility principle asks whether a class has one coherent reason to change. Responsibilities arise from the concerns and policies it serves, not simply the number of methods. A cohesion graph connecting methods that share fields can expose clusters, but shared state is only a clue. Methods can share a field while serving unrelated purposes, and a coherent responsibility can use several data structures.

The split-class exercise asks which changes should remain independent. Separating storage, formatting or domain calculations can reduce the number of clients affected by a change. The historical Date API example illustrates the long-lived cost of mixing concerns in a public library. Compatibility limits cleanup after release, so careful boundaries matter. Avoid splitting every method into its own object; the goal is a coherent model with understandable responsibilities and interfaces.
chapters.prediction: If every method touches the same field, has SRP been proved?
chapters.explanation: No. Shared fields suggest structural cohesion but do not establish a single policy or reason to change.
chapters.narration: Single responsibility concerns coherent reasons to change. Use method relationships and shared fields as clues, then ask which stakeholder or policy drives each change. Splitting responsibilities can improve maintainability, but excessive fragmentation can obscure the model. Public libraries add compatibility costs, making clear boundaries especially valuable before clients depend on them.
chapters.focus: Reasons to change, method/field cohesion graph, splitting responsibilities and date API evolution.

chapters.title: Design for extension
paragraphs: The painter example initially knows how to draw each concrete shape. Adding a triangle requires another branch or loop in the painter, spreading the variation into a client. Introducing a Shape operation moves drawing behavior behind a shared contract. The painter can then iterate over shapes without naming every concrete type, making the supported extension point explicit.

Open–closed design protects stable behavior from selected kinds of change; it does not forbid editing code or demand inheritance for every extension. Composition, strategies and registration can serve the same purpose. Adding a shape may still require creation or configuration changes elsewhere. The key question is whether the abstraction matches the expected variation, and whether its contract is sufficient for new implementations to work without special cases in the client.
chapters.prediction: After introducing Shape.draw, must every file remain unchanged when Triangle is added?
chapters.explanation: No. The painting loop can remain stable, while Triangle and its creation or registration still need implementation.
chapters.narration: The open–closed principle encourages stable code around deliberate extension points. In the shape example, a common drawing operation keeps the painter independent of concrete shape types. This does not eliminate all edits or require inheritance everywhere. Judge the abstraction by the changes it localizes and the contract new implementations must satisfy.
chapters.focus: Replace shape-type branches with a Shape abstraction; consider anticipated axes of change.

chapters.title: Substitutability and contracts
paragraphs: Substitutability concerns behavior visible to clients. If a client works under a supertype contract, replacing an object with a subtype should not invalidate those expectations. A subtype must not demand stronger preconditions or provide weaker guarantees. Phrase this through implications: every input accepted by the supertype must remain acceptable, and the subtype’s successful outcome must satisfy the supertype’s promised result.

The mutable Rectangle example promises independently adjustable width and height. Square breaks that promise by changing both dimensions in a setter, so a client expecting area fifty receives one hundred. This is a contract problem rather than a statement about geometry. The unmodifiable List example needs different care: Java documents optional mutators, so an exception can be permitted by the declared contract. A client requiring mutation needs a stronger capability guarantee.
chapters.prediction: Does the mathematical fact that every square is a rectangle prove mutable Square is a behavioral subtype?
chapters.explanation: No. The programming interface’s mutation promises, not just geometric membership, determine substitutability.
chapters.narration: Liskov substitution preserves the expectations clients are entitled to make. The mutable Rectangle and Square example fails because setters violate independent-dimension behavior. Check actual preconditions, results and invariants. Exceptions are not automatically violations: optional operations may allow them. The right question is whether the subtype honors the contract the client was promised.
chapters.focus: Rectangle/Square, preconditions/postconditions and the limits of optional operations.

chapters.title: Client-focused interfaces and dependency inversion
paragraphs: Interface segregation focuses on what each client needs to depend on. A broad interface can mix reading, writing and event handling even when many clients need only one role. Smaller role interfaces make capabilities clearer. An adapter with default no-op callbacks may reduce implementation effort, but it does not erase the conceptual breadth of the original interface.

Dependency inversion places policy behind stable abstractions instead of binding it directly to implementation details. JDBC illustrates application code using a database-facing API implemented by drivers. The boundary can localize many implementation changes, while behavioral differences and contract changes may still affect clients. Together, these principles encourage focused contracts owned by the needs of the caller, with concrete implementations replaceable only to the extent that they preserve those contracts.
chapters.prediction: Does adding an interface guarantee callers are unaffected by every implementation change?
chapters.explanation: No. Changes in observable behavior, contract or supported capabilities can still affect callers even when method signatures remain stable.
chapters.narration: Design interfaces around client roles and put high-level policy behind appropriate abstractions. Read-only and mutable capabilities need not be bundled for every client. JDBC shows how a stable API can separate application logic from driver details. These boundaries reduce coupling, but only a preserved behavioral contract makes replacement safe.
chapters.focus: Role interfaces, listeners/adapters, abstraction boundaries and JDBC.

quiz.question: A painter iterates over Shape objects and calls draw. What changes when Triangle is added?
quiz.answer: Add a Triangle implementation and arrange its creation/registration; the generic painting loop can remain unchanged if the Shape contract suffices.

quiz.question: Why does Square fail the mutable Rectangle client that sets width=5 then height=10 and expects area=50?
quiz.answer: Its setters change both dimensions, violating the client-visible contract that the dimensions can be changed independently.

quiz.question: Is UnsupportedOperationException from an unmodifiable List necessarily a violation of its documented List contract?
quiz.answer: No. List specifies optional mutating operations; the client must require/support mutability explicitly. Separate read and write interfaces can make that requirement clearer.

These are teaching conventions rather than universal rules: associations may also be represented as properties; nested classes include static classes; notes can annotate more than methods. Clarify modeled lifetime ownership versus language garbage collection.
Pattern book date differs (1995 versus 1994). Verify publication/edition context or avoid the date in quizzes.
Shared fields are a cohesion heuristic, not proof of SRP. Client-specific method exposure also anticipates ISP.

“Only 4 functional methods” is too narrow; the Date API has additional operations. java.time was inspired by Joda-Time but is not simply the same library renamed; verify official API history before reuse.
OCP does not forbid all edits to production code or require inheritance-only extension. Teach stable abstractions around anticipated variation; composition is a valid mechanism.

Use logical implication for contract strength, not ambiguous subset/superset wording. Rectangle need not require unequal dimensions; the square setter need not always change old height. The reliable violation is breaking the promise that setWidth leaves height unchanged.

Slides 55–58 call unmodifiable List an LSP violation, while slide 64 acknowledges mutators are optional in the declared List contract. Present this as an interface-design tradeoff and a mismatch with a client assuming mutability, not an unconditional violation of the documented contract.
No-op/throwing methods are investigation signals, not automatic violations: MouseAdapter itself legitimately provides empty callbacks.
DIP reduces coupling to implementation details but does not make Layer A immune to every change in Layer B, especially behavioral or interface changes.

exercise.prompt: A report class calculates grades, formats HTML, writes SQL, and sends email. Propose boundaries and interfaces, then explain one benefit and one cost. Show how adding a PDF renderer affects the design.
exercise.answer: Separate grading policy, rendering, persistence, and delivery where they change for different reasons. Depend on narrow interfaces at the policy boundary. A PDF renderer can implement the rendering contract without changing grading logic. Do not create an interface for every trivial method: extra abstractions carry navigation and maintenance costs. Test behavior and substitutability.

units.title: Requirements & quality attributes
units.description: Translate stakeholder concerns into clear requirements and measurable quality scenarios that guide design.

chapters.title: Discover the problem and its stakeholders
paragraphs: Requirements begin with stakeholders who have needs, constraints and competing priorities. Elicitation gathers these concerns; analysis examines consistency, feasibility and completeness; specification records an agreed account; validation checks that the account addresses the actual problem. A request to use a particular technology may reflect a real operational constraint, or it may be a proposed solution that hides the underlying need.

Ask why a statement matters and who is affected if it is unmet. Distinguish a business goal from an observable system behavior and from a contractual or organizational constraint. A system boundary helps expose missing actors and dependencies. Conflicts should become explicit tradeoffs rather than being concealed in vague wording. Architecture then starts from a clearer problem, avoiding detailed optimization of a solution that stakeholders never needed.
chapters.prediction: A stakeholder says “use Java.” Is that automatically a functional requirement?
chapters.explanation: No. It is a technology constraint or proposed solution; discover its rationale and whether it is actually mandatory.
chapters.narration: Requirements work establishes what problem the system must solve and whose concerns matter. Gather needs, examine conflicts and feasibility, then validate the specification with stakeholders. Ask why a technology or deadline is required. Clear boundaries and explicit priorities give architectural decisions a defensible starting point.
chapters.focus: Elicitation, conflicting goals, feasibility and the difference between needs and solution constraints.

chapters.title: Write specifications people can test
paragraphs: A specification bridges stakeholder needs and implementation. It may describe functions, data, interfaces, quality constraints, operating environments and delivery obligations. Good requirements are understandable, consistent, verifiable and traceable to goals. Completeness does not mean unlimited detail; it means including what is necessary for the intended agreement and identifying unresolved questions instead of hiding them.

Ambiguity becomes visible when different readers can produce different valid interpretations. Soup or salad and bread has more than one grouping; a name that “can be 127 characters” leaves optionality and length boundaries unclear. Rewrite statements so a tester can distinguish compliance from noncompliance. Preserve links to rationale and design choices, because changing a requirement after deployment may affect architecture, tests, training and operational procedures as well as code.
chapters.prediction: Can two reviewers agree that a sentence sounds reasonable yet disagree about an implementation passing it?
chapters.explanation: Yes. Missing boundaries, definitions and acceptance criteria allow incompatible interpretations; testable examples help expose them.
chapters.narration: A useful specification connects real needs to observable acceptance conditions. Review wording for ambiguity, consistency and traceability. Examples such as character limits reveal missing boundary conditions. When a requirement changes, follow its links into design, implementation and tests so the update remains coherent rather than producing a locally correct but incompatible feature.
chapters.focus: Scope, data/interfaces, quality criteria, ambiguity and traceability.

chapters.title: Classify requirements and quality attributes
paragraphs: Functional requirements describe what the system does, while quality requirements constrain how well relevant behavior occurs under stated conditions. Delivery or technology constraints form additional categories. These categories do not determine priority: a quality requirement can be essential, and a proposed function can be optional. “Secure login” needs decomposition into authentication behavior and explicit security properties rather than a stronger adjective.

Quality attributes often span multiple responsibilities. Reliability can depend on persistence, retries, status reporting and recovery; performance can depend on database work, communication and workload. They therefore influence architecture, even though the system can continue evolving after an initial design. Express these concerns in scenarios and acceptance checks. Asking how an attribute is observed makes it easier to compare designs and prevents quality from becoming a list of aspirations.
chapters.prediction: Is a two-second response requirement less mandatory because it is nonfunctional?
chapters.explanation: No. Mandatory status depends on the agreement and system context, not whether the requirement describes a function or a quality attribute.
chapters.narration: Separate behavior, quality and other constraints, then assign priorities explicitly. Quality requirements often cross component boundaries and shape architecture. Replace words such as fast or secure with scenarios and observable checks. Functional and quality requirements can both be mandatory, and both need clear evidence of satisfaction.
chapters.focus: Functional behavior, quality attributes, constraints and architecture-wide effects.

chapters.title: Make quality measurable
paragraphs: A measurable requirement names the observation and the conditions under which it must hold. The search example gives a proportion and a latency threshold, but still needs a workload, dataset and measurement window. Counting registered users does not specify concurrency or request intensity. Define how failures, timeouts and warm-up periods enter a measurement so that different tests answer the same question.

Other qualities require equal care. Accuracy needs a defined error measure; maintainability needs a relevant change task or evidence rather than a vague hope. XML, Java or a SQL database may be design constraints, but they do not by themselves establish interoperability. Distinguish the objective from a proposed mechanism and choose a test that addresses the objective. Any additional numerical targets in a teaching exercise should be marked as assumptions.
chapters.prediction: Do twenty million registered users imply twenty million simultaneous requests?
chapters.explanation: No. Registration, activity, concurrency and request rate measure different things and require separate workload assumptions.
chapters.narration: Turn quality goals into measurable agreements. State the metric, workload, threshold and observation interval, including how failures are counted. Capacity needs an activity model, not just a user total. For other attributes, distinguish an outcome from a prescribed technology and test the outcome that stakeholders actually care about.
chapters.focus: Operationalize latency, accuracy, capacity, maintainability and interoperability.

chapters.title: Optimize the system rather than isolated parts
paragraphs: The C1, C2 and T1 example models producers feeding a consumer on one CPU. Under the stated teaching assumptions, each stage operation has equal cost and completed throughput is limited by the smaller of combined production and consumption. A CPU budget of twelve stage operations per second must cover both producing and consuming work, so maximizing each component independently is not a valid objective.

With producer rates three and three and a consumer rate six, completed throughput is six while the total CPU budget is twelve. Giving all three components four operations per second consumes the same budget but only completes four because consumption is slower than production. This is a deliberately simplified capacity model. Real systems add scheduling, unequal costs and queueing; one hundred percent utilization leaves no headroom and should not be described as unlimited capacity.
chapters.prediction: Why can rates 3,3,6 beat rates 4,4,4 with the same CPU cost?
chapters.explanation: Both consume twelve stage operations per second, but throughput is min(C1+C2,T1): six in the first case and four in the second.
chapters.narration: Optimize the end-to-end flow, not isolated component rates. In this simplified producer-consumer model, throughput is limited by combined production or consumption, whichever is smaller. Balancing the stages can outperform equal allocations. State the equal-cost assumption and remember that full CPU utilization is still a capacity limit, with no practical headroom.
chapters.focus: Producer/consumer pipeline and a shared CPU budget; identify assumptions and end-to-end throughput.

quiz.question: Rewrite “the system should be fast” as a verifiable search requirement.
quiz.answer: For example: under a specified workload and dataset, at least 95% of search requests complete within 2 seconds over a stated measurement window; define how errors count. Numbers are a proposed teaching example, not a source requirement.

quiz.question: Why is “20 million users” not a sufficient capacity requirement?
quiz.answer: It does not say whether these are registered, daily active or concurrent users, what requests they issue, or what latency/error objectives must hold.

quiz.question: In the slide’s producer/consumer model, C1=3, C2=3, T1=6 operations/s. What are throughput and CPU use?
quiz.answer: Throughput=min(3+3,6)=6 completed requests/s; CPU consumption=3+3+6=12 stage operations/s, or 100% of the stated budget. This depends on equal per-operation cost and the stated flow.

review.issue: Both examples use “secure”; separate a concrete authentication function from a measurable security constraint so the distinction is not just adding “highly”.
Functional requirements are not inherently all mandatory, nor quality requirements optional. Priority and mandatory status are separate dimensions.
The claim that NFRs cannot be expressed in use-case form is too absolute; quality constraints and scenarios can accompany use cases. The 20% figure lacks attribution.

Specify workload, observation interval, percentile and failure treatment for latency; “20 Million Users” needs concurrent/registered distinction. “Within 90% of actual cost” is ambiguous; replace with an explicitly defined error bound only after confirming intent. “24 hrs to ruin” is a typo for run.
XML, Java, SQL and no triggers are solution constraints, not sufficient measurable evidence of interoperability. Explain the distinction.

The arithmetic is coherent only under an explicit model: C1 and C2 produce work consumed by T1, stage operations have equal CPU cost, and throughput=min(C1+C2,T1). Clarify that 12 refers to stage operations per second, not completed end-to-end requests. At 100% CPU, “No bottleneck” should mean balanced stage rates, with CPU still limiting capacity; practical queueing/headroom is omitted.

exercise.prompt: Rewrite “the registration system must be fast and reliable” as two testable quality scenarios. Include a burst of traffic and a lost response after saving. Explain which architectural decisions each scenario influences.
exercise.answer: Specify workload, environment, stimulus, expected response, measurement window, and threshold. For example, define a response-time percentile under a stated arrival rate, and require retry with the same ID to recover a durable saved result after response loss. Numbers must come from stakeholder needs, not this example. These requirements influence capacity, admission control, persistence, and idempotency.

units.title: Scalability, services & HTTP
units.description: Move from a program to a concurrent service, identify resource limits, and trace an HTTP request through a web application.

chapters.title: From programs to services
paragraphs: An algorithm solves a problem for an input; a service repeatedly accepts requests from users. Complexity still matters, but a fast individual request does not guarantee a healthy service under many simultaneous requests. Requests compete for CPU, memory, disks, network capacity and shared data. Measure throughput together with latency and errors, and specify the workload.

Concurrent users describe how much activity overlaps, while requests per second describe a rate. Monthly active users describe audience size and say little about a sudden burst. As an example, a registration portal can have modest daily use but a large opening-minute surge. The architectural question is whether it can absorb that surge while keeping response times and correctness acceptable.
chapters.prediction: If a service doubles its throughput but response time grows tenfold, has it necessarily scaled successfully?
chapters.explanation: No. Throughput alone hides queueing and user experience; the result must meet a stated latency and error target.
chapters.narration: A museum catalogue runs a fast image lookup in isolation. During a school booking event, however, 600 visitors arrive together and compete for the same database connections. The lookup algorithm has not changed, but its operating conditions have. A service must keep accepting work over time, share finite resources among requests, and respond acceptably while arrivals overlap. A successful single-user demonstration therefore does not establish service capacity. Begin the capacity discussion with a workload: which operations arrive, how often, and with what acceptable latency and error rate? Suppose browsing costs much less than exporting a collection. Two tests at 200 requests per second can produce very different results if their operation mixes differ. Record both completed throughput and response-time distributions, including slow requests. Then increase arrivals until waiting or errors rise. This experiment distinguishes an audience-size claim from evidence that the architecture can support a particular demand.
chapters.focus: Capacity depends on workload and latency, not audience size alone.

chapters.title: Scaling up and scaling out
paragraphs: Vertical scaling adds capacity to an existing machine: more memory, faster storage or more CPU resources. Horizontal scaling adds machines. The first often keeps coordination simpler; the second opens more capacity but requires work distribution, shared-state management and failure handling. Neither guarantees proportional improvement. The bottleneck determines whether the next resource is useful.

Threads can overlap IO waits even on a single CPU core. A blocked worker is waiting rather than performing useful CPU work, allowing another to run. CPU-bound tasks need actual execution resources for parallel speedup. Before buying capacity, inspect whether work waits for storage, exhausts CPU, competes for memory or contends on shared locks. A larger machine cannot remove every architectural limit.
chapters.prediction: Will doubling CPU cores necessarily halve request latency?
chapters.explanation: No. IO waits, serial work, locks and external dependencies can dominate.
chapters.narration: The museum first considers a larger machine and then a second application replica. If image processing consumes all available CPU, more cores may help when the work can run in parallel. If every request waits on the same database lock, another application machine can simply create more waiting. Vertical and horizontal scaling are changes to resource allocation; whether either helps depends on the resource or coordination point currently limiting useful work. Consider a worker that spends 10 milliseconds computing and 40 milliseconds waiting for a remote response. On one core, another request can use CPU during that wait, so concurrency can improve utilization without making the first computation faster. This is not a promise of a fivefold speedup: network limits, scheduling and shared dependencies still matter. Before choosing larger machines or additional replicas, measure CPU use, waiting time and contention. After changing capacity, repeat the same workload test to see whether the bottleneck moved elsewhere.
chapters.focus: Diagnose the bottleneck before adding cores or replicas.

chapters.title: Request processing and HTTP
paragraphs: A service framework accepts network messages and routes them to application logic. The slide worker loop takes a request from a queue, performs work and queues a response. Empty queues can block readers; full bounded queues can block producers or trigger rejection. These details matter during overload: unlimited waiting can consume memory and create unacceptable response times.

HTTP defines request and response semantics. A request includes a method, target and fields, and may include content. A response includes status and fields and may include content. The textual example illustrates HTTP/1.1. Frameworks can implement concurrency using threads, processes or asynchronous event handling; the request-response contract does not require one specific execution model.
chapters.prediction: What happens if requests enter faster than workers can finish them for a sustained period?
chapters.explanation: The queue grows unless bounded; latency rises, and a bounded system eventually rejects or slows arrivals.
chapters.narration: Follow a catalogue request through an arrival queue, application handling and a response. When all workers are busy, another request waits rather than receiving an immediate worker. If arrivals remain faster than completions, the queue grows. A bigger queue may absorb a short burst, but it does not create processing capacity. Bounded queues make overload explicit and let the service reject or defer work instead of allowing unlimited memory growth and increasingly late answers. The client sends an HTTP method, target and fields, with optional content; the service returns a status, fields and optional content. A framework translates that contract into application calls and manages network activity. It might use threads, processes or asynchronous handlers. Those choices affect how waits are managed, but they do not change the meaning of GET or a response status. In a design review, draw both the public request contract and the internal queues: one explains interoperability, while the other explains what users experience during a burst.
chapters.focus: Trace the contract and queues as separate design concerns.

chapters.title: A Wikipedia request, end to end
paragraphs: In the supplied historical Wikipedia example, the browser requests an article and MediaWiki produces HTML. The application retrieves wiki text, converts it to markup, adds page structure and may add a personalized header. The database stores durable article data while application instances execute rendering logic. This separation explains why the system has more than just a web server.

Trace which work repeats across readers. The article body may be shared, but identity-dependent content may differ. That distinction motivates the next unit on caching and stateless workers. The historical architecture diagram is a teaching model rather than an inventory of current Wikimedia infrastructure. Repeated diagram-build slides can become one step-by-step request walkthrough with each component highlighted in turn.
chapters.prediction: Can the entire personalized HTML response always be reused for another visitor?
chapters.explanation: No. Shared article content and user-specific response content require different reuse policies.
chapters.narration: Apply the chapter’s rendering pipeline to a different service: a museum collection page. A browser requests an exhibit; the application reads its description from durable storage, formats the description, adds navigation and returns HTML. The database owns saved content, while the application constructs a representation for a reader. Labelling these responsibilities makes the architecture diagram useful: each arrow should identify a request or data transfer, rather than simply connecting boxes. Now compare two visitors reading the same exhibit. They can share the description and public image, but one visitor’s private saved-list indicator must not become the other visitor’s answer. This observation identifies possible reuse boundaries before choosing a cache. Trace a second request after an exhibit description changes, and explain which component must observe that update. The point of the historical diagram is this method of reasoning about repeated computation, durable state and personalized output; its component names are not a prescription for a modern deployment.

exercise.answer: Two workers cap ideal throughput at 10; four workers move the cap to the database at 12. At a steady arrival rate of 15, the queue continues to grow. Measure throughput, tail latency, errors, CPU, database wait time, and query costs under a reproducible workload. units.title: Stateless services, proxies & caches
units.description: Make worker state explicit, understand intermediary roles, and reason about cache hits, eviction, and stale data.

chapters.title: Where does state live?
paragraphs: State is information retained across operations. A worker with local session or game state cannot automatically be replaced by any other worker, because another instance may lack that information. The SMTP conversation illustrates a protocol interaction whose later commands depend on earlier commands. A self-contained HTTP request provides a useful contrast, but HTTP applications can still maintain state.

A stateless application worker does not require durable per-client memory in that specific worker between requests. It may consult a changing database or perform writes. This is different from a pure function: stateless deployment does not imply deterministic output or absence of side effects. Locate the state explicitly before deciding whether a request can move to a different instance.
chapters.prediction: If two stateless workers read a database at different times, must they produce identical responses to the same URL?
chapters.explanation: No. Shared data, time or randomness can change; statelessness concerns worker-local conversational state.
chapters.narration: A bicycle rental application remembers an unfinished booking in worker A’s memory. The customer’s next request reaches worker B, which has never seen the booking. Both workers run identical code, but they are not interchangeable for this interaction because their retained information differs. Calling the protocol HTTP does not remove that dependency: application state can exist above a stateless request protocol. Identify the information needed for the next operation and locate its authoritative copy. A stateless worker may still read changing data and perform writes. For example, it can accept a booking identifier, load that booking from shared storage and update it there. The worker does not need the customer’s previous requests to have visited that same process. This distinction separates deployment statelessness from a mathematical pure function. To test your design, replace the worker between consecutive requests. If another healthy worker can continue using the request and shared services, the application has avoided a hidden dependency on the original process.
chapters.focus: Replace the worker mentally to expose hidden session state.

chapters.title: Stateless workers with stateful data
paragraphs: The chess example begins with games stored in an application dictionary. Replicating the process produces separate dictionaries, so a player must reach the instance holding the game. If that instance fails, its in-memory games may be lost. Moving authoritative game data to shared storage allows another application instance to continue a request.

This moves coordination rather than eliminating it. Two concurrent moves need validation and an atomic or version-checked update. The shared database may become a capacity or availability bottleneck. Cookies similarly carry information with a request, often an opaque reference to session data. Signed claims can be verified without a lookup, but signing does not hide their contents or solve every expiry and revocation problem.
chapters.prediction: Does moving a chess game to a database by itself prevent two concurrent moves from overwriting each other?
chapters.explanation: No. The update must enforce the game rules with appropriate transactions, conditions or version checks.
chapters.narration: Move the bicycle booking into shared storage, and a replacement worker can retrieve it after a restart. That improves replaceability but exposes a second question: what if two workers reserve the final bicycle concurrently? If both read availability before either writes, each may believe the reservation is valid. Shared storage solves access to a common record; a suitable atomic operation or version check must also protect the booking rule. For example, worker A reads booking version 12, while worker B changes it to version 13. A conditional update based on version 12 should now fail rather than silently overwrite B’s change. The application can reload and explain the conflict. A session cookie can identify the customer whose request is being processed, but it does not itself enforce inventory correctness. Explain these responsibilities separately: the request carries identity or a session reference, shared storage retains durable state, and the update protocol decides which concurrent change is accepted.

chapters.title: Proxies and cache hits
paragraphs: A proxy forwards requests to another component and returns responses. A caching proxy can sometimes answer using a saved representation; a load-balancing proxy selects among backends. These roles can coexist but are distinct. The intermediary itself needs capacity and availability planning, even if forwarding costs less than generating a dynamic page.

A cache hit avoids an expensive fetch; a miss obtains the value from backing storage and may insert it. Eviction frees space when capacity is limited. LRU evicts the least recently accessed entry, so an access trace lets you predict behavior. In cache-aside designs application code manages lookup and fill; transparent designs hide these steps behind the normal data-access interface.
chapters.prediction: With capacity two, after accesses A, B, A, which item does inserting C evict under LRU?
chapters.explanation: B, because A was accessed more recently.
chapters.narration: Trace a cache with room for two exhibit descriptions through accesses A, B, A, C, B. A and B initially miss and fill the cache. The second A is a hit and makes A the most recently used entry. C then misses and evicts B under least recently used eviction. The final B misses and evicts A. Only one of these five accesses hits, showing that a cache’s benefit depends on access order and capacity, not merely on its existence. In a managed cache design, application code performs this lookup and fill around storage access. With a caching proxy, the client uses its normal request interface while the intermediary manages eligible reuse. Both still need a valid key and freshness policy. A load-balancing proxy performs a different decision: which backend should receive work that must be forwarded? One component may implement both roles, but a diagram should make clear whether it is selecting a worker, serving saved content, or doing both.

paragraphs: Trace a cache with room for two exhibit descriptions through accesses A, B, A, C, B. A and B initially miss and fill the cache. The second A is a hit and makes A the most recently used entry. C then misses and evicts B under least recently used eviction. The final B misses and evicts A. Only one of these five accesses hits, showing that a cache’s benefit depends on access order and capacity, not merely on its existence.

In a managed cache design, application code performs this lookup and fill around storage access. With a caching proxy, the client uses its normal request interface while the intermediary manages eligible reuse. Both still need a valid key and freshness policy. A load-balancing proxy performs a different decision: which backend should receive work that must be forwarded? One component may implement both roles, but a diagram should make clear whether it is selecting a worker, serving saved content, or doing both.

chapters.title: Popularity, freshness and HTTP caching
paragraphs: Skewed demand makes caching powerful: a small popular set can account for much of the request volume. The long tail contains many rarely requested items. A high hit rate depends on workload, cache capacity and freshness policy; it is not guaranteed by adding a cache. Personalized or rapidly changing content can limit safe reuse.

Writes make saved copies potentially stale. TTL bounds freshness only under its assumptions; invalidation needs reliable delivery and race handling; immutable versioned names avoid overwriting the same representation. HTTP adds explicit caching controls. Distinguish no-cache, which permits storage but requires validation before reuse, from no-store. Private responses must not become shared-cache answers for other users.
chapters.prediction: Can a cache with a 95% hit rate still be incorrect?
chapters.explanation: Yes. A high hit rate can serve stale or identity-inappropriate data; correctness and hit rate are separate.
chapters.narration: Suppose an exhibit launch receives 800 eligible reads each second and the measured cache hit ratio is 85 percent. Under a simple model with one backing read per miss and no revalidation traffic, only 120 reads per second reach the backing service. This gain follows from repeated demand for reusable content. If requests become personalized or spread across many rarely repeated items, the same cache may achieve a much lower hit ratio. Freshness is a separate decision. A public exhibit description might tolerate a short stale interval, while a reservation confirmation needs a different policy. Versioned image names let old and new images coexist without changing an existing cache entry. For mutable responses, distinguish expiration, validation and storage prohibition. No-cache can allow storage but requires successful validation before reuse; no-store forbids storage. A private response cannot become a shared-cache answer simply because it has a long freshness lifetime. Always explain whose requests are allowed to reuse an entry.

chapters.title: Why state moves into the database
paragraphs: Moving session and application state out of a web process makes that process easier to duplicate. The shared database now carries durable data and coordinates changes made by those copies. This is useful separation of concerns, but it also concentrates work. Trace a page request through the application to distinguish computation, database lookup and storage access before deciding where additional servers help.

Storage systems trade access latency against capacity. Caches and RAM keep frequently needed data close to computation; persistent storage retains the larger dataset. RAID can combine disks for capacity, throughput or redundancy, depending on configuration. More disks do not eliminate the CPU, memory bandwidth and I/O limits of the database server controlling them.
chapters.prediction: If we double stateless app servers, must throughput double?
chapters.explanation: No. All copies may still wait on the same overloaded database or storage path.
chapters.narration: Adding another application server is useful only if application work is the limiting step. Let us follow a booking request through the shared data service and estimate its capacity before changing the architecture. A repair-booking service runs on six application servers. Each booking needs three database operations. If the database sustains 1,800 such operations per second, the idealized ceiling is 600 bookings per second, regardless of how many otherwise idle application servers are added. This estimate assumes equal operation costs and no competing workload; measurements must check those assumptions. Now suppose a frequently read parts catalogue fits in the database buffer cache. Repeated reads may avoid storage access, but writes, locks and network transfers still consume resources. Adding disks could improve storage throughput without fixing a CPU-bound query or a contended record. Separate durable storage, coordination and query execution when explaining why the database remains busy after the web tier scales.

chapters.title: Relational models and query execution
paragraphs: A relational schema describes tables, columns and relationships. A staff row can refer to one department, and a department can refer to one building. Keeping shared facts in their own tables avoids updating the department name separately for every employee. A JOIN reconstructs the information needed by a particular application view without requiring that view to dictate the storage layout.

The database contributes more than persistence. It can enforce keys and constraints, coordinate concurrent changes, index data and run filtering or aggregation near storage. Ordinary files provide naming, permissions and durable bytes, but application code must add many higher-level guarantees. Choose the abstraction by the behavior required, rather than assuming a file and a table are interchangeable.
chapters.prediction: If a department changes name, how many authoritative rows should change?
chapters.explanation: With the shown normalized schema, one department row changes; staff references retain the same department identifier.
chapters.narration: The relational model separates facts that have different owners and lifetimes. A useful design exercise is to reconstruct one screen from those facts, then ask both what it means and how much work it requires. A bicycle library stores Bicycle, Branch and Loan tables. Each bicycle refers to its current branch, and each loan refers to one bicycle and one borrower. Renaming a branch changes one branch record rather than every bicycle description. A loan-history page joins those records to display useful information without storing a duplicate branch name in every loan. For a query asking for one borrower’s active loans, the database can first identify a small set of matching loans and then look up their bicycles. Reading every bicycle before filtering could do much more work. The execution plan reveals the chosen access path; the schema alone does not guarantee it. Also decide whether the page should display the branch’s current name or preserve its historical name when the loan occurred.

chapters.title: Indexes and their costs
paragraphs: An index stores an additional access path to rows. Without a suitable access path, a query may scan many rows to find a small result. Tree indexes organize keys for equality and ordered range access; hash indexes organize equality lookup. Real database indexes usually use page-oriented structures suited to storage, rather than the simple binary tree used to introduce the idea.

Every index consumes space and must be maintained when indexed data changes. A composite index also has an order: an index beginning with firstName generally favors predicates involving firstName. A lastName-only query may behave differently depending on optimizer and data. Examine the execution plan and measure the representative workload before adding an index, then check its effect on writes as well.
chapters.prediction: Will an index on every column always improve a busy system?
chapters.explanation: No. It can increase write maintenance and storage cost without helping the queries that dominate the workload.
chapters.narration: Think of an index as a route through data designed for a particular question. We will choose one for a parcel service and then account for the extra work that the route creates. A parcel service frequently asks for a particular depot’s shipments created during the last hour. An ordered index on (depot_id, created_at) groups one depot’s entries and then narrows the time interval. A query for all depots during that hour may need a different plan because its predicate omits the leading column. The optimizer and data distribution determine the actual access path. Suppose that targeted query examines 240 index entries instead of scanning 800,000 shipment rows. That is a promising reduction in examined data, not a guaranteed latency ratio. Every inserted shipment must also update the index. Compare execution plans and measured response times before and after the change, including ingestion throughput, index size and unusually busy depots. An index is a maintained copy of ordering information, not free acceleration.
