chapters.title: Read scaling and failover
paragraphs: A primary database can stream changes to read replicas. Each replica maintains a copy of the dataset and can answer eligible reads, so many read requests no longer compete for the primary. Asynchronous replication creates lag: a successful write does not mean every replica already exposes it. A profile page that immediately reloads from a lagging replica may appear to lose the edit.

Read replicas do not automatically spread write execution or increase the capacity of an individual full copy. Cascading replication can reduce direct fan-out from the primary but adds propagation stages. A standby can improve recovery after failure, but safe promotion requires more than detecting a timeout: the system must decide authority and prevent competing primaries from accepting incompatible changes.
chapters.prediction: After saving a profile, is any replica safe for the immediate confirmation page?
chapters.explanation: Only if its consistency policy ensures it has the required write; otherwise use an appropriate primary or session-aware read.
chapters.narration: Replication introduces two separate architectural questions: where reads can run, and which machine is authorized to accept writes. We can scale the first without automatically solving the second. Start by classifying the promises made to each reader. A tutoring service updates a student’s appointment time on the primary database. A replica that has not yet applied the change still returns the old time. The write can have succeeded even though an immediately refreshed page looks unchanged. Historical appointment reports may tolerate this delay; the confirmation shown to the student should follow a path that satisfies the promised freshness. Imagine one primary handling 400 writes and 3,000 reads per second. Moving 2,400 eligible reads to three replicas leaves roughly 600 reads on the primary, but each replica must still apply the write stream. This is a workload sketch, not a capacity guarantee. If the primary fails, promoting a standby requires establishing a single writer and understanding which acknowledged writes it contains. A timeout alone does not establish that the previous writer has stopped.

chapters.title: Sharding and fan-out
paragraphs: Sharding assigns disjoint subsets of rows to different database partitions. A useful key places the data for a common operation together while distributing storage and traffic. With user_id modulo two, Steve’s profile and posts can live on one shard. That makes a single-user query local, but it does not make every query local: friends may belong to every partition.

A friends feed may request candidate posts from multiple shards and merge them into one ordered result. This costs network work and coordination. Under a balanced equal-cost model, N nodes each serving C operations per second support about NC/k requests when each request touches k nodes. A request touching every node eliminates that ideal throughput gain, although parallelism may still reduce one query’s latency.
chapters.prediction: Does adding more shards necessarily accelerate a global top-ten feed?
chapters.explanation: No. Each feed may still contact every shard, and the coordinator must merge results; skew and network cost can also grow.
chapters.narration: Sharding distributes different records rather than making full copies. Its benefit depends on keeping common operations local. Let us follow a customer query, then compare it with a global report using a deliberately simple capacity model. A maintenance platform shards equipment records by customer. Fetching one customer’s inspection history stays on a single shard, while a report across all customers contacts several shards and merges their results. Placing customers evenly by count can still overload a shard containing a huge customer; traffic and record size matter as well as the routing rule. In a simplified balanced model, eight shards each provide 500 equal-cost operations per second. Requests touching one shard have an upper bound near 4,000 requests per second. If each request touches four shards, the bound drops to about 1,000. If it touches all eight, it drops to 500. Parallel requests may finish sooner than serial requests, but each still consumes cluster work. Cross-shard updates additionally need an explicit atomicity or reconciliation strategy.

The shard key trades locality against balance. Read replicas share read load but may lag and do not inherently distribute writes or increase per-replica data capacity.

chapters.title: Data locality and denormalization
paragraphs: Think of a relational dataset as a graph: rows are vertices and references are edges. Partitioning tries to balance the data while cutting few frequently traversed edges. An even row count is not enough if one row is exceptionally popular or a relationship triggers many downstream reads. Access frequency and query shape belong in the partitioning decision alongside storage size.

Denormalization duplicates or embeds data so a common query can retrieve an aggregate locally. A profile document can contain its positions and education rather than requiring a chain of lookups. The cost appears during updates: a shared label copied into many documents must be changed consistently if that is required. NoSQL does not universally forbid references; embedding is a modeling choice with trade-offs.
chapters.prediction: Will copying an industry name into every profile make renaming the industry easier?
chapters.explanation: No. It can make profile reads local, but the rename now affects many copies or requires accepting temporary disagreement.
chapters.narration: Data locality begins with the question a user asks, but it must also account for how facts change. We will use campsite reservations to distinguish useful snapshots from duplicated information that becomes difficult to maintain. A campsite booking page needs a reservation, its selected facilities and a short site description. Embedding a snapshot of the booked facilities can make that page a single aggregate read. Keeping the current site description separately avoids rewriting thousands of reservations whenever the description changes. The correct boundary depends on whether the page promises historical booking details or the latest catalogue information. Suppose 2,000 reservations contain a copied access instruction. A correction now requires updating many copies or accepting mixed versions during propagation. By contrast, a historical price agreed at booking should usually remain a snapshot. Denormalization is therefore a choice about update ownership and meaning, as well as query speed. List each embedded field, its authoritative source and the rule for changing it before celebrating fewer network lookups.

chapters.title: Hash partitioning
paragraphs: A deterministic hash maps a key to a value in a fixed hash space. Partition owners can divide that space into ranges; a client or routing layer hashes a requested key and selects its owner. This separates routing from the original key’s spelling or numeric value. The simplified model gives direct access to a key without consulting every machine.

Hash partitioning does not automatically balance traffic. Thousands of different keys may distribute well while one famous profile attracts most reads. Equal ranges also need not contain equal-sized values. Hash indexes suit equality access but discard the original ordering needed for efficient ranges. Use the key-value model to understand partitioning, while remembering that real database families can add secondary indexes and richer query operations.
chapters.prediction: If one key receives half of all requests, will a better hash spread those requests?
chapters.explanation: No. All requests for that key still map to its owner or replica set unless the application introduces another distribution or caching strategy.
chapters.narration: A hash gives a repeatable route from a key to a partition. It is a routing mechanism, not a proof of balanced performance. Let us trace one identifier and then test the assumptions behind the distribution. Consider a toy hash space with values zero through ninety-nine, divided into four equal ranges. A parcel identifier hashing to sixty-two is routed to the owner of the fifty-through-seventy-four range. The client needs the current ownership map as well as the hash function. When ownership changes, migration and routing must agree so requests do not silently read the wrong place. Evenly distributed identifiers do not imply evenly distributed traffic. If one parcel receives half the tracking requests, its owner can remain overloaded while other owners are idle. Adding machines does not split that individual key’s requests automatically. Similarly, hashes scatter nearby timestamps, so a query for all parcels created between two times cannot simply walk adjacent hash values. Separate point lookup, range lookup and hot-key mitigation when evaluating the design.

chapters.title: Replication and partitions
paragraphs: Partitioning spreads different data across machines; replication stores multiple copies of each partition. Replication allows a system to keep a copy when a machine fails, but a change reaches replicas at different times. A read may therefore see an older version unless the system coordinates the read with the required writes. Network partitions make this coordination problem more severe.

During a partition, a distributed service cannot guarantee both linearizable operations and a successful response to every request at non-failing nodes. A majority side may continue while a minority refuses certain operations. Alternatively both sides may accept operations and require reconciliation. This is a conditional trade-off about partition behavior, not a claim that all distributed systems permanently choose any two desirable features.
chapters.prediction: Can both sides of a 2+1 split independently accept arbitrary writes while guaranteeing one real-time order?
chapters.explanation: Not while also remaining available for every request; they cannot coordinate the conflicting decisions across the partition.
chapters.narration: Replication provides extra copies, but those copies may be unable to communicate. The architectural decision becomes concrete when we ask what the application may promise while communication is broken. Compare a rental commitment with a display preference. A tool-rental service keeps three copies of an availability record. A network break isolates one copy from the other two. If both sides independently confirm rental of the final drill, later reconciliation cannot make both promises physically possible. A design protecting that single-item invariant may require the isolated side to refuse or delay the booking while the majority continues. A less critical observation, such as a customer’s preferred display colour, may be accepted on both sides and reconciled later. This illustrates the CAP trade-off during a partition: linearizable behavior and a successful response to every request at non-failing nodes cannot both be guaranteed. It does not say replication is always unavailable or always inconsistent. State the operation, its invariant and the failure condition rather than assigning one slogan to the entire application.

chapters.title: Session guarantees
paragraphs: Session guarantees describe what one client should experience. Monotonic reads prevent that client from moving back to an older version. Read-your-writes requires later reads to include its completed writes or subsequent changes. Monotonic writes preserve the order of that client’s writes. These promises are useful even when the system does not provide a single globally consistent view to everyone.

Routing a session to one up-to-date replica can help, but failure or movement to another replica can break the assumption. More robust designs carry a version or progress token and wait for a replica that has reached it. Arbitrarily sleeping is not a correctness guarantee because propagation delay has no fixed bound. State the promised property explicitly and test the failure transition.

chapters.explanation: Monotonic reads. Read-your-writes is also broken if version 8 represented that client’s own completed write.
chapters.narration: Session guarantees describe what one client may observe across requests. They are more precise than saying that data is eventually consistent. Follow one inspection report as its reader changes replicas, and name the guarantee broken at each step. A field technician saves inspection version twelve and then reads the report through another replica that has reached only version eleven. Returning eleven violates read-your-writes. Later, after the technician has seen version thirteen, returning twelve violates monotonic reads even if twelve includes the technician’s own earlier change. These guarantees protect different parts of the user’s experience. One design attaches a progress token to the session. A chosen replica serves the read only after reaching the required progress, or the request moves to a suitable replica. In this simplified single-record example the token can be a version; multi-partition systems need richer tracking. Pinning a session can reduce switches but does not by itself handle replica failure. Waiting a fixed number of milliseconds is also insufficient because replication delay is not bounded by that timer.

chapters.title: Quorums and their limits
paragraphs: For one key replicated N times, a write may wait for W acknowledgements and a read for R responses. If R+W>N, the selected sets overlap. With three replicas and two acknowledgements for both operations, a read quorum intersects a completed write quorum. This is the useful intuition behind quorum diagrams, but the reader must still interpret versions correctly.

Overlap alone does not prove linearizability under concurrent writes, incomplete operations, changing membership or clock skew. The protocol must resolve those cases. Quorum sizes also affect availability: with one of three replicas unavailable, two-of-three reads and writes can still obtain enough responses, while a write requiring all three cannot. A large cluster remains scalable by using a bounded replica set per key.
chapters.prediction: For N=3, R=1 and W=3, what stops when one replica fails?
chapters.explanation: New writes cannot obtain all three acknowledgements. Reads may still obtain one response, subject to the system’s consistency and failure rules.
chapters.narration: Quorum diagrams help us reason about which copies must meet. The arithmetic is useful precisely when we keep its assumptions visible. Work through a five-replica example, then separate set intersection from the stronger guarantee we may want. A record has five designated replicas. A write waits for acknowledgements from three, and a read obtains responses from three. Every possible pair of those sets overlaps because three plus three exceeds five. If two replicas are unreachable, the remaining three can still supply the required responses, assuming they are mutually reachable and the protocol’s other conditions hold. Changing the policy to five write acknowledgements and one read response also creates overlap, but now one unavailable replica prevents writes. Neither arithmetic rule alone specifies how a reader handles different versions, concurrent writes or a write that reached some replicas before its client timed out. Those require protocol rules. Apply the calculation to the replica set for this record, not to the total number of machines in a large partitioned cluster.

chapters.title: Stronger consistency and synthesis
paragraphs: Linearizability makes each operation appear to take effect at one instant between its invocation and completion. Its operation order must respect real-time precedence: when one operation finishes before another begins, the later operation cannot be placed before it. Concurrent operations can be ordered either way when the result remains legal for the object being modeled.

Preserving each client’s local sequence is weaker than preserving this cross-client real-time relationship. Monotonic reads, monotonic writes and read-your-writes are valuable session guarantees, but their combination is not a definition of linearizability. For an architectural decision, start with the invariant: a collaborative counter, seat reservation and activity feed may need different guarantees, even if each uses replication.
chapters.prediction: A write finishes before another client starts a read. May a linearizable read return the prior value?
chapters.explanation: No, unless a later intervening operation legally restored that value; the completed write must precede the later read.
chapters.narration: To evaluate a consistency claim, draw when each operation starts and finishes. A legal explanation must respect completed operations that precede later calls. This small history makes the difference between session behavior and linearizability visible without relying on slogans. A depot changes a gate code from A to B. The update completes before a different operator begins a read. For a linearizable register with no intervening write, that read must return B. If the read overlapped the update, returning either value might be legal, depending on where the operations take effect within their execution intervals. Now let both operators remain on separate replicas. Each may see an internally sensible sequence while the second operator still reads A after the completed update. Preserving each client’s order does not enforce this cross-client real-time relationship. A linearizable read also cannot guarantee that a later, separate action uses current data: another write can occur between them. Protecting a combined business operation may require a suitable transaction or conditional update in addition to clear read semantics.

review.issue: NoSQL defined as no references, no schema, one table and one indexed key.
review.correction: Scope this to a teaching key-value model. NoSQL is a family; document/wide-column stores can have schemas, references, secondary indexes and richer queries. Do not define NoSQL by absent joins.

review.issue: Hashing implies no bottlenecks and exact equal data/work distribution.
review.correction: Hash distribution is approximate; hot keys, value size, network, rebalancing and coordination constrain scaling. MD5 demonstration is not a security recommendation.

review.issue: Hexadecimal ranges have inconsistent digit widths and replication diagrams disagree.
review.correction: Use consistent 00000000–3fffffff,40000000–7fffffff,80000000–bfffffff,c0000000–ffffffff. Define replica ownership explicitly rather than transcribing conflicting ranges.

review.issue: CAP pick two and centralized SQL as solution to both timeliness and consistency.
review.correction: State the trade-off specifically during network partitions. Centralization does not guarantee bounded latency or availability. Staleness from ordinary lag is not itself a network partition.

review.issue: MongoDB does not replicate.
review.correction: False: MongoDB replica sets replicate data and support primary election.

review.issue: Quorum overlap with client timestamps treated as sufficient for consistency.
review.correction: State fixed replica-set, completed-write and version-order assumptions. Overlap alone is not a general linearizability proof; concurrent/incomplete writes and clock skew need protocols.

review.issue: Program-order preservation called linearizability; three session properties equated with it.
review.correction: Linearizability additionally respects real-time precedence across clients. Session guarantees are weaker; present them separately.

review.issue: HDFS, BigTable and S3 all described as DHT filesystems.
review.correction: Treat these as different distributed storage designs. Avoid asserting common hash routing or filesystem semantics without product-specific evidence.

exercise.prompt: A key has three replicas. Compare R=2,W=2 with R=1,W=3 when one replica becomes unreachable. State what you can and cannot conclude about consistency.
exercise.answer: Both choices satisfy R+W>N, so successful read and write quorums overlap in the simple fixed-replica model. With one unreachable replica, R=2,W=2 can still meet both quorums; R=1,W=3 can read but cannot complete its configured write quorum. Overlap alone is not a proof of linearizability. Discuss version ordering, concurrent writes, repair, and the failure assumptions.

units.title: Choosing a data store
units.description: Choose storage by workload and correctness requirements, from transactions to analytics, search, documents, and objects.

chapters.title: Start with workload and invariants
paragraphs: Choose storage by describing the application’s operations before choosing a product. Record the shape and size of the data, lookup keys, range queries, joins, update rates and required guarantees. Course registration needs to protect seat counts; lecture recordings need efficient delivery of large objects; course notes may need ranked text search. One application can have several distinct storage workloads.

A product category is a starting point, not a complete decision. Relational schemas can evolve, document stores can validate fields, and many systems combine capabilities. Evaluate the operations that must be atomic, the acceptable staleness and the team’s operational constraints. Using several stores is useful only when their ownership and update paths are clear enough to maintain.
chapters.prediction: Should video files and seat reservations necessarily use the same persistence interface?
chapters.explanation: No. Large-object delivery and concurrent invariant-preserving updates have different access patterns and can justify different stores.
chapters.narration: Storage selection is an architectural argument about the application, not a contest between database labels. Start with a small set of operations and their promises. Then choose the least complicated arrangement that can meet and operate those promises. A community workshop needs to reserve machines, search project descriptions and serve tutorial photographs. Reservations must not overlap for the same machine. Search can tolerate a short indexing delay, while photographs are large immutable objects once published. These are three access patterns within one product; the shared user interface does not imply identical storage requirements. Begin with a relational reservation store and object storage for photographs, then evaluate whether its existing text-search capability is sufficient. A separate search service becomes worthwhile only when requirements justify its indexing pipeline and recovery work. Record expected request rates, acceptable staleness, atomic operations and who operates each component. A technically capable store may still be a poor choice if the team cannot back it up, diagnose failures or restore it within the required time.

chapters.title: Transactions and concurrency
paragraphs: A checkout updates several related facts: the order, its line items and the remaining gift-card balance. Atomicity means these changes commit together or roll back together. It does not, by itself, make a read-then-write sequence safe from another checkout. Two transactions can read the same balance and compute competing replacements unless the chosen isolation or update protocol prevents it.

One approach locks the gift-card row before checking and changing the balance. Another performs a conditional decrement that succeeds only when sufficient balance remains, checks the affected-row result and keeps the order changes in the same transaction. The application must handle conflicts and rollback. A hand-written distributed spin lock is not a substitute: it also needs ownership, expiry and crash-recovery semantics.
chapters.prediction: Does adding BEGIN and COMMIT to the slide’s plain SELECT then overwrite necessarily stop double spending?
chapters.explanation: No. The operation needs appropriate isolation, locking or an atomic conditional update, plus balance validation and failure handling.
chapters.narration: A transaction groups changes, while its isolation and update protocol determine how concurrent requests interact. We can see the distinction with a single projector. Follow the successful path, the competing request, and then the failure that occurs halfway through. A makerspace has one spare projector. Two requests each read available_count equal to one and both attempt a booking. Wrapping each request’s statements in a transaction gives all-or-nothing changes, but does not by itself specify isolation strong enough to prevent both from making the same decision. The read-and-update interaction needs deliberate concurrency control. One approach conditionally decrements the count only when it is positive, checks whether exactly one row changed, and creates the reservation in the same transaction. The database’s supported atomic update semantics must ensure competing updates are evaluated safely. The losing request reports unavailability rather than inserting a booking. If creating the reservation fails, the decrement rolls back. Retried requests also need a way to recognize an already committed booking rather than silently creating a second one.

chapters.title: Storage models and analytics
paragraphs: Operational transaction processing usually consists of many small reads and writes, such as fetching a student’s enrolments or reserving a seat. Analytics may scan years of records to compare enrolment trends. A column-oriented layout can read just the relevant columns and compress similar values effectively, making it attractive for broad aggregations over large datasets.

This distinction concerns workloads, not an absolute ban on indexes or a requirement that every analytical query use many machines. Analytical copies may be refreshed through ingestion pipelines and lag behind operational state. Explain that freshness before using a dashboard for an immediate decision. Running aggregation near storage also avoids sending every raw row to the application merely to calculate a small result.
chapters.prediction: For a three-year average grouped by location, why might reading columns beat fetching complete rows?
chapters.explanation: The calculation needs only selected attributes, so reading and compressing those columns can reduce I/O substantially.
chapters.narration: One dataset can support both immediate operations and broad analysis, but those workloads ask the hardware to do different work. Trace the columns required by a dashboard and then compare its freshness needs with the live delivery service. A delivery dashboard computes average journey time by district from 120 million events. It needs district, duration and date, but not the driver’s notes or the full delivery address. A column-oriented representation can read a smaller relevant subset and compress repeated values. The final result may contain only a few dozen rows, so aggregation near storage avoids transferring the entire event collection. The operational service instead checks and updates one delivery’s state repeatedly throughout the day. That is a different access pattern, even if both stores accept SQL. If analytics imports events every fifteen minutes, a dashboard can omit recent completed deliveries without either database being broken. Display the data’s freshness and use the operational source for decisions that require current state. Benchmark representative queries rather than assuming a storage layout makes every query faster.

chapters.title: Documents, search and wide-column stores
paragraphs: A document store can keep a nested profile as one aggregate, with a configured shard key controlling distribution. A search engine serves another need: locating documents by terms and relevance. An inverted index maps each term to matching document identifiers. A query for Watertown AND gift intersects those posting lists instead of scanning every document’s text.

Wide-column and key-value designs are often shaped around known partition keys and within-partition ordering. Sensor readings might group by device and a bounded time interval, then order by timestamp. A good design considers partition size and hot devices as well as lookup convenience. Product feature lists in the source are historical; the durable lesson is to align the storage abstraction with the actual query.
chapters.prediction: How would a basic inverted index answer a two-term AND query?
chapters.explanation: Find the document-ID list for each normalized term and return their intersection.
chapters.narration: Different storage models make different questions inexpensive. We will compare text retrieval with time-ordered sensor data and make the lookup steps explicit. The useful choice follows the operation, including how derived structures are kept up to date. A museum stores exhibit descriptions as documents. For keyword search, an inverted index might map “bronze” to documents {4, 9, 12} and “river” to {9, 15}. Their intersection returns document 9 for a query requiring both words. This explains retrieval mechanics, but ranking and language handling need additional rules. Updating the document also requires updating its searchable representation. For temperature readings, a different design uses sensor_id and day as the partition key and observation_time as the within-partition ordering key. This supports one sensor’s daily range query while bounding partition growth. Searching every sensor for one interval may need another access path. A search index can lag its source, and a telemetry partition can become hot. Neither a document shape nor a key-value interface removes these workload and consistency questions.

chapters.title: Caches and memory data structures
paragraphs: An application cache stores values that help construct responses, such as a leaderboard or precomputed summary. An HTTP reverse-proxy cache stores reusable responses at a different layer. These may coexist: an uncached personalized page can still reuse a cached shared fragment. Define which store owns the authoritative data and how cached copies expire or are invalidated.

In-memory systems can expose structures such as sets, counters and sorted sets, reducing the work required to update a small part of a value. Persistence, expiry and eviction depend on configuration; they are not determined solely by calling a product a cache. A rebuildable cache and a durable database have different recovery requirements even when they use the same software.
chapters.prediction: If a leaderboard cache disappears, should authoritative course records disappear too?
chapters.explanation: No. If it is designed as a rebuildable cache, the source records remain elsewhere and the leaderboard can be recomputed.
chapters.narration: A cache is part of a data flow, not merely a faster machine. Explain where its values come from, how they become stale and how they recover. Our recreation-centre example separates a helpful display from an authoritative booking decision. A recreation centre shows a cached count of available places on its home page. The count can be briefly stale, but the booking operation checks the authoritative reservation store. This separates a fast informational view from the decision that commits scarce capacity. A time-to-live limits how long one cached value remains eligible; it does not make that value current at every instant. For a weekly activity ranking, a sorted-set abstraction can update one participant’s score without rewriting the entire ranking. Before adopting it, decide whether the ranking can be rebuilt from durable events and what happens after eviction or restart. Also plan how simultaneous cache misses avoid overwhelming the origin. A reverse-proxy cache of a whole public page sits at a different layer from these application-managed values, even when both reduce repeated work.

chapters.title: Files, objects and final selection
paragraphs: A mounted network filesystem provides a file interface that existing applications can use. Block storage instead exposes volumes on which a filesystem may be built; object storage exposes named objects through service APIs. These are distinct abstractions. EFS is file storage, while EBS is block storage. Object storage is a natural fit for lecture media addressed through delivery URLs.

Distributed processing historically benefits from moving computation close to data, as illustrated by HDFS. Other designs separate compute and object storage, so locality is one consideration rather than a universal requirement. Finish the selection with a small architecture: identify the owner of each dataset, the access path, consistency needs and recovery process, then explain why a simpler arrangement would or would not suffice.
chapters.prediction: Can an application replace any mounted filesystem with an object bucket without changing behavior?
chapters.explanation: Not necessarily. It must check required file operations and semantics against the object API and adapt its access pattern.
chapters.narration: Files, objects and blocks expose different operations to applications. Choose the interface by following a real workflow, including partial failure. A wildlife recording archive helps us connect storage selection with the responsibilities that appear between two independent services. A wildlife archive stores short audio recordings as objects and keeps their searchable metadata in a database. Clients request a recording by an object identifier rather than mounting the archive as a disk. A legacy analysis program that expects directories and file operations may instead need a filesystem interface. A block volume provides lower-level storage on which a filesystem can be created; it is not itself a shared file service. The recording and its metadata form a cross-system workflow. If an upload succeeds but the metadata write fails, the archive needs a cleanup or retry rule so abandoned objects do not accumulate. If metadata is published before upload completion, users may receive broken links. Draw these failure paths before adding stores. The final architecture should identify ownership, identifiers, access control, recovery and the reason each separate abstraction is necessary.

review.issue: EBS listed as a network filesystem.
review.correction: EBS is block storage; EFS is file storage. Keep object, file and block abstractions distinct.

review.correction: Describe the single-primary relational design in the slides rather than every SQL system. SQL is a query language and relational data model does not dictate one write topology.

review.issue: _id always sharding key; journaling preserves document history.
review.correction: The shard key is configured and need not be _id. Journaling supports crash recovery, not application version history.

chapters.title: HTTP as an API contract
paragraphs: An API specifies how another program requests work and interprets results. HTTP-based APIs use methods, targets, fields, status codes and optional bodies. The weather example combines a location parameter with a JSON response. A useful contract documents units, missing values and errors as well as the successful payload.

Choose methods according to their semantics: GET retrieves a representation, PUT creates or replaces state at a known target, POST asks a resource to process supplied content, and DELETE removes the target association. Status codes help clients distinguish success, missing resources, forbidden access and server failure. HTTPS protects transport; avoid putting credential examples in URLs that may be logged or copied.
chapters.prediction: Is a JSON body alone enough to specify a reliable API contract?
chapters.explanation: No. Methods, resource identity, status/error behavior, authentication and data meaning also matter.
chapters.narration: A maintenance service exposes GET /tickets/731. A successful response includes a ticket identifier, a status and an estimated duration. The JSON shape alone is insufficient: clients need to know whether duration means minutes or seconds, whether a missing estimate is null or omitted, and what happens when a ticket is unavailable. An API contract therefore includes meaning and failure behavior as well as a syntactically valid example. Choose the method before inventing an endpoint name. A read should not close the ticket as a side effect. A replacement request to a known ticket target differs from submitting a new work request for the service to process. Document authorization failures and absent resources so clients can react appropriately. Use HTTPS for transport protection, and avoid placing access tokens in example query strings that might appear in logs. chapters.title: Retries and resource identity
paragraphs: Retries are normal when a client cannot tell whether an operation completed. Idempotence means repeating an identical request has the same intended server effect as sending it once. It does not require the same response status. Deleting an already removed resource may report that it is missing without deleting anything else.

The delete-latest example fails this requirement because the target changes after the first deletion. A stable post identifier lets retries refer to the same item. Similarly, a PUT to a chosen document ID replaces that target, while POST creation may allocate a fresh ID each time unless the application provides deduplication. Resource-oriented naming helps communicate intent, but nouns alone do not define the REST architectural style.

chapters.narration: A client submits a repair request and loses its connection before receiving the response. It cannot tell whether the server committed the work. Retrying is therefore an uncertainty problem, not proof that the first attempt failed. A stable target helps: repeating a request to set ticket 731 to the same intended state can be designed to have the same intended effect as one attempt. That does not require identical response bytes or status codes. Contrast this with an operation that closes whichever ticket is currently oldest. After the first success, a retry could close a different ticket. The resource identity moves, so repetition changes the intended effect. Use an explicit ticket identifier for that operation. chapters.title: Serialization and references
paragraphs: Serialization turns structured values into bytes that can cross a network or be stored. JSON provides objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. XML uses elements and attributes with well-formed syntax. Correct examples matter: JSON forbids trailing commas, and an empty XML element must close explicitly or use self-closing syntax.

An in-memory graph is not always a simple nested tree. Repeating shared objects wastes space, and recursively nesting a cycle never ends. Emit each object once with an identifier, then encode relationships using those identifiers. Readers resolve references under an agreed schema. The byte dump illustrates ASCII-compatible UTF-8 text; characters beyond ASCII may require multiple bytes, so character count and byte count can differ.

chapters.explanation: Naive recursive serialization never terminates; IDs turn the cycle into finite references.
chapters.narration: Two maintenance tickets refer to the same building, and that building record refers to its active tickets. Naively nesting the entire building inside each ticket duplicates data. Following the building’s ticket references recursively can also create an endless cycle. The in-memory structure is a graph, while ordinary nested JSON values form a tree. Serialization must decide how to represent identity and relationships instead of blindly walking every pointer. One representation emits building B9 once, emits tickets T1 and T2 once, and links each ticket with buildingId B9. The client resolves those identifiers using the agreed response structure or additional API requests. Also distinguish text length from byte length: a title containing accented characters can occupy more UTF-8 bytes than its character count. Schema choices, reference rules and encoding all belong to the data exchange contract.

chapters.title: Choosing a protocol
paragraphs: HTTP offers widely available clients, servers, status semantics and caching infrastructure. HTTPS adds encrypted transport. Reuse can lower implementation effort, but API authors must understand caching and retry semantics instead of treating HTTP as an arbitrary message tube. Framework capabilities differ, so database pooling or deployment security should not be assumed automatically.

Separate architectural style, serialization and transport. REST describes architectural constraints; JSON and Protocol Buffers encode data; gRPC is an RPC framework that commonly uses Protocol Buffers with HTTP/2. Binary encoding therefore does not imply avoiding HTTP. Choose based on interoperability, tooling, streaming, payload size and measured performance requirements. Smaller messages alone do not settle the architecture decision.

chapters.title: One deployable application
paragraphs: A monolith is one application deployment boundary, even when many identical instances run behind a load balancer. The MediaWiki example makes this clear: two hundred interchangeable replicas improve capacity without dividing business responsibilities into distinct services. External databases and caches do not by themselves change that application boundary.

A monolith can simplify local execution, integration and transactions. Its challenges can include coordinating many contributors and deploying a large application for a small change. These are tradeoffs rather than inevitable defects: strong module boundaries can support a maintainable monolith. Evaluate the team, change patterns and operational needs before introducing network boundaries simply to make a diagram look more distributed.
chapters.prediction: Does adding a second identical application instance create a second microservice?
chapters.explanation: No. It creates another replica of the same application.
chapters.narration: A repair platform contains ticketing, technician scheduling and customer notifications in one deployable application. Running four copies behind a load balancer creates four replicas of that application. It does not create four business services. Each replica can still execute all three responsibilities, and a release typically deploys the same application package. A database and cache outside that package do not, on their own, establish independent application boundaries. This arrangement can be useful for a small team: developers run one application locally, follow a request through one process and use a local database transaction for related changes. Trouble may appear when unrelated modules force coordinated releases or compete for very different resources. First ask whether clearer modules inside the application would address the problem. A network boundary adds deployment and failure concerns, so justify it using an observed need for independent change or operation rather than the visual appeal of additional boxes.

chapters.title: Choosing service boundaries
paragraphs: Service boundaries assign responsibilities to separate deployable applications. Each exposes a contract that clients can use without knowing its implementation language. This can enable specialized scaling and independent development, but only when changes can actually occur independently. A set of services that must always release together retains strong coupling.

Network boundaries introduce latency and partial failures. A successful payment with a failed inventory update cannot automatically be undone by a local database rollback. Designs need explicit retry, idempotence and recovery behavior. Debugging also crosses process boundaries. Smaller units may simplify focused tests while increasing the importance of contracts, observability and integration testing. Use business responsibilities and consistency requirements to justify a split.

chapters.explanation: Independent deployment; the system retains release coupling despite network separation.
chapters.narration: Suppose technician scheduling becomes a separate service because its optimization workload and release cadence differ from ticket management. The boundary now has a contract: ticket management requests a slot, scheduling accepts or rejects it, and both agree on identifiers and outcomes. This can allow independent implementation, but independence is weakened if every schema change still forces both services to release together. A meaningful boundary contains change as well as code. Now scheduling accepts a slot but the reply is lost. Ticket management sees a timeout while scheduling has already changed state. A local rollback in ticket management cannot undo a remote commitment automatically. The design needs a way to discover the outcome, avoid duplicate reservations and recover from abandoned work. Trace this failure before celebrating a successful normal-path demo. Smaller services can make focused tests easier, while cross-service behavior requires contract tests, observability and explicit recovery policies. Compare these costs with the independence that motivated the split.

chapters.title: Teams, mocks and multiple clients
paragraphs: Teams can agree on an API before implementing each side. A mock dependency lets client work proceed, but a mock represents assumptions rather than proof of compatibility. Define inputs, outputs, status behavior and error cases, then test those expectations against the real service. Instant, always-successful mocks hide timeouts and failures that matter in production.

The same backend API can support a browser, mobile app and desktop app. In a server-rendered design the backend prepares HTML; in an SPA much presentation logic runs in the browser and obtains data through APIs. Real applications can combine both approaches. Separating clients from services helps reuse, while authorization and validation must still be enforced by the server for every client type.

A mock accelerates collaboration because it makes assumptions executable; it does not prove that the dependency behaves that way in production. chapters.title: One service, many workers

paragraphs: A public archive adds three application workers behind one service address. With round robin, six incoming requests can be distributed two per worker. That sounds balanced until one request generates a large export while the others read a small record. Equal request counts do not imply equal work or equal completion times. A routing policy uses observable signals, and those signals are only approximations of the capacity each worker has available.

Next ask whether workers are interchangeable. If an export’s progress exists only in worker A’s memory, sending a follow-up request to B may fail even though B is healthy. Durable progress in shared storage can allow replacement, but that storage now needs its own capacity and failure design. The balancer gives clients a stable entry point and can hide worker membership changes. It does not remove every dependency behind that entry point. Follow one request to storage and back before claiming that adding workers has multiplied end-to-end capacity.

chapters.title: Local routing: L4 and L7

paragraphs: The archive serves metadata and large scans through the same HTTPS hostname. If routing must distinguish /records from /scans, some component must inspect HTTP information. An ordinary IP-and-port decision cannot see that distinction inside encrypted application traffic. An HTTP-aware reverse proxy can terminate TLS, inspect the path and select an appropriate worker pool. It may establish a second encrypted connection upstream; termination does not require leaving the internal hop unprotected.

For a generic transport service, a layer-four balancer may be a better fit because it routes using connection information without interpreting HTTP resources. NAT is one implementation, not the definition of layer-four balancing. Likewise, a reverse proxy need not wait for an entire document before forwarding it: streaming and buffering depend on implementation and configuration. Compare designs using the features required by this workload, then benchmark realistic payloads, connections and security settings. Historical throughput examples should not become universal limits for either layer.

chapters.title: Failures and safe deployments

paragraphs: The archive runs four workers, each measured to handle 100 requests per second for a specified workload. At 280 requests per second, removing one worker leaves a nominal capacity of 300. That small margin may be inadequate once request costs vary or a dependency slows. A rolling deployment needs spare capacity as well as a sequence of replacement steps. Stop new assignments, allow existing work to drain within a deadline, deploy, and verify readiness before returning the worker.

A failed health probe is evidence that the checked path did not respond acceptably; it is not proof of a process crash. Overload, network trouble or a dependency can produce the same observation. Failure thresholds reduce reactions to brief disturbances but delay removal, so some requests may fail before routing changes. Explain what clients may retry and with what limit. During a rolling update, old and new versions coexist, which makes API and storage compatibility part of deployment safety rather than an optional cleanup task.

chapters.title: DNS and global discovery

paragraphs: A resolver receives Region East with a 90-second TTL at time zero. At time 20, the authoritative policy switches new answers to Region West. Under the simplified ordinary-cache model, a lookup at time 50 can still receive East from the resolver’s cache; the answer becomes eligible for refresh at time 90. Updating the authority changes future answers, not every previously distributed copy at the same instant.

Existing connections add another layer: a client may continue using an established connection without repeating DNS for every request. Multiple clients may also share one resolver, so a single cached answer can direct a large group. Geographic steering often estimates location from the resolver or partial client-network information, rather than knowing each user’s precise position. Treat DNS as a discovery mechanism with caching behavior. Combine it with regional load balancing and an explicit data recovery strategy; changing a name-to-address answer does not by itself make another region ready to accept writes.

chapters.title: CDNs and anycast

paragraphs: The archive publishes a scanned map under an immutable versioned URL. If 2,000 eligible map requests arrive per second and edge caches serve 92 percent as fresh hits, a simplified model sends about 160 fetches per second toward origin. This estimate excludes validation and other traffic, but it shows the source of the benefit: saved content answers repeated reads near users. A private account page is a different object and cannot safely share the same reuse policy.

Anycast answers a different question: which network location receives traffic for an address advertised from several sites? Routing chooses a path using network policy and topology, not a guarantee of geographic nearness. A CDN can use anycast, DNS steering and caching together. Cache directives still determine whether an answer may be reused, and route changes still need handling for established connections. A private directive excludes shared-cache storage of the whole response; a long max-age does not override it. Distinguish traffic steering, content reuse and application correctness when reviewing an edge design.

chapters.narration: The archive publishes a scanned map under an immutable versioned URL. If 2,000 eligible map requests arrive per second and edge caches serve 92 percent as fresh hits, a simplified model sends about 160 fetches per second toward origin. This estimate excludes validation and other traffic, but it shows the source of the benefit: saved content answers repeated reads near users. A private account page is a different object and cannot safely share the same reuse policy. Anycast answers a different question: which network location receives traffic for an address advertised from several sites? Routing chooses a path using network policy and topology, not a guarantee of geographic nearness. A CDN can use anycast, DNS steering and caching together. Cache directives still determine whether an answer may be reused, and route changes still need handling for established connections. A private directive excludes shared-cache storage of the whole response; a long max-age does not override it. Distinguish traffic steering, content reuse and application correctness when reviewing an edge design.

chapters.title: Design review and self-check

paragraphs: Design an archive service for the morning a newly digitized collection opens. Public scans can use versioned URLs and edge caching, while requests to reserve the last available research-room seat must reach application logic and authoritative storage. Draw DNS discovery, the edge, a regional entry point, workers and storage. Label where a read may be answered without contacting origin and where a write must be checked against current state.

Now fail one worker during the surge and one region during a reservation. Explain the delay before health information changes, what happens to in-flight requests and which clients might still use cached DNS answers. A retry must not create two reservations, and a second worker must not allocate the same final seat concurrently. Those requirements need an explicit data and operation contract, not just another load balancer. A convincing design combines routing, capacity, freshness and recovery assumptions, then tests the failure cases that could violate them.

chapters.title: Read the case architecture and its interfaces
paragraphs: The National Gun Violence Memorial case is a historical publishing-system example. A servlet application renders public pages, supports contributions and provides volunteer administration. The architecture connects a SQL database, object storage, CDN, scraper, email and payment services. Follow one read and one write through those responsibilities to explain the design before proposing additional infrastructure. The supplied picture describes the teaching case, not a verified current deployment.

The endpoint examples use action-oriented names and HTML forms. Rewriting a deletion as DELETE /victim/{id} makes the resource-oriented intention clearer, but an API style cannot be assessed from spelling alone. Authentication and authorization must still protect administrative actions. The schema captures records, photographs, comments, moderation, sessions and editing history; indexes and uniqueness constraints reveal important access patterns and integrity rules that should survive a redesign.
chapters.prediction: Does changing an administrative URL to DELETE /victim/{id} make the operation authorized?
chapters.explanation: No. HTTP semantics and naming do not replace authentication or authorization checks.
chapters.narration: Use a hypothetical city history archive to practise reading a deployment diagram. A visitor requests a public exhibit page. The application reads descriptive records from a relational database, renders the page, and includes image URLs delivered through a media service. A curator uploading a replacement image follows a different path: authenticate the curator, check editing permission, store the object, and update its metadata. One diagram contains both paths, but their failure and permission requirements differ. Mark every crossing with the information it carries. The object store receives bytes, while the database receives identifiers, captions and relationships. The browser receives a presentation rather than unrestricted database access. If image storage succeeds but the metadata update fails, an unreferenced object can remain; if the metadata points at a missing object, the public page breaks. This small example makes interfaces concrete and exposes coordination questions before introducing more servers. Naming an endpoint after a resource helps readers, but does not settle these consistency or access-control obligations.

chapters.title: Place media, caching and operating cost in context
paragraphs: The case stores original images, thumbnails and archived pages in object storage while retaining relational metadata in SQL. Separate representations support different display sizes and allow a CDN to serve repeated media requests. Randomized object names may reduce easy guessing, but do not create authorization. Public access is a permission choice; private or restricted content needs an explicit access policy and appropriate delivery mechanism.

The deck reports April 2020 traffic and operating expenses to connect workload characteristics to infrastructure cost. Those values are historical measurements, not a current quotation for the same service. Cost depends on storage, compute, requests and transfer patterns, while caching changes both origin load and where delivery is charged. Use the figures to reason about the original tradeoff, and obtain fresh prices and workload assumptions before estimating a new deployment.

chapters.explanation: No. Anyone with a publicly accessible URL may retrieve it; access permissions determine authorization.
chapters.narration: An archive has a two-megabyte photograph but displays a small preview in its search results. If one thousand searches each download the original, that is about two gigabytes of image transfer before protocol overhead. A forty-kilobyte preview reduces the same illustrative workload to roughly forty megabytes. Storing multiple representations spends some storage and processing to reduce repeated transfer. The relational record can identify each representation while object storage holds the bytes. Next distinguish a cache hit from an origin fetch. A media cache can reduce repeated origin work, but total cost still depends on the charging model for storage, requests and delivery. Build a worksheet with quantities first and insert current prices only when preparing an actual estimate. A historical cloud bill is evidence about one workload and configuration, not a promise for the archive. Private images also need a permission design: an unpredictable filename alone does not establish who may fetch an object.

chapters.title: Scale the read path deliberately
paragraphs: The proposed 200-fold traffic increase motivates changes in several places. Read replicas distribute eligible database reads, larger instances increase individual capacity and multiple stateless application instances accept requests through a load balancer. These changes solve different constraints. A replica does not automatically absorb writes to the primary, and adding application instances does not remove a database bottleneck or inconsistent local state.

Caching HTML and media can avoid origin work entirely when users can share responses and tolerate suitable freshness. Define cache keys, invalidation and exclusions for administration or personalized content. Read replicas may lag their source, so classify operations by whether stale reads are acceptable. The final design remains a monolithic application distributed across instances: scaling deployment does not require dividing business logic into independently managed microservices.
chapters.prediction: Will doubling application instances necessarily double completed requests when the database is saturated?
chapters.explanation: No. The limiting shared resource remains; measure demand and address that constraint.
chapters.narration: Suppose a public archive receives one thousand page requests per second. If a shared cache answers eighty percent, two hundred requests reach the application. If each remaining page needs three database reads, the uncached read workload is approximately six hundred reads per second. These are deliberately simplified assumptions, but they show why cache effectiveness must be applied before sizing the database. Adding application workers changes application capacity; it does not by itself change those six hundred reads. Classify the remaining requests before distributing them across replicas. A visitor reading an old exhibit may tolerate a short delay, while a curator checking an edit immediately after saving expects the new state. The first path can use a lagging replica if the product permits it; the second may require a primary read or another explicit consistency mechanism. A scalable diagram therefore needs routing rules as well as boxes. Measure the hit rate and query count under a representative mix rather than assuming every request benefits equally.

chapters.title: Evaluate scaling claims with workload evidence
paragraphs: The source estimates eighty million monthly write-related events after scaling, or roughly thirty per second when averaged over 2.6 million seconds. That arithmetic is a starting point, not a peak-load model. One user action may cause several physical I/O operations or a transaction, while indexes, logging, batching and caching influence the cost. CPU counts and storage IOPS cannot be translated directly into proportional application throughput.

The case is comparatively cache-friendly because most traffic reads shared pages, visitors are not personalized and some visible effects can be delayed. Memorial records grow differently from page views, so traffic growth need not multiply dataset size. These are workload properties to verify rather than universal facts about publishing sites. Use measurements, service demands, peak scenarios and failure cases to evaluate capacity, and preserve integrity even when writes do not need complex cross-record business transactions.
chapters.prediction: Is thirty average writes per second enough to choose the database instance?
chapters.explanation: No. Peak rate, per-write work, indexes, consistency, durability and competing reads also matter.
chapters.narration: An illustrative service records twenty-six million updates over a thirty-day month. Dividing by approximately 2.6 million seconds gives ten updates per second on average. That calculation is useful for checking magnitude, but it conceals timing. If a news event produces one hundred updates per second for several minutes, a system sized only for the average can accumulate a backlog or reject requests despite apparently modest monthly traffic. Also expand the meaning of an update. One user action may write a primary row, update indexes and append an audit record inside a transaction. Those actions do not map to a fixed number of physical disk operations because buffering, logging and storage behaviour intervene. Test the complete transaction with realistic data, contention and burst duration. Report latency and error rate alongside throughput. The decision to retain one primary should follow those measurements and consistency needs, rather than a direct comparison between user events and a device's advertised operations per second.

units.title: Push notifications and connected clients
units.description: Connect devices, choose a delivery channel, and route notifications across changing connections.

chapters.title: Why the server cannot simply call the phone
paragraphs: A ride arrival or an auction bid happens because another participant acts. The recipient needs an update without repeatedly asking whether anything changed. Yet a phone is not an ordinary public server: its address changes, NAT and firewalls restrict inbound connections, and the application may be suspended. Email and SMS provide useful notification channels, but do not replace every in-app interaction.

The architectural requirement is therefore a reachable delivery path, not merely an HTTP endpoint on the device. An outbound connection can establish that path while the device is online. Offline periods still require a policy for retaining, expiring or replacing messages. Distinguish notifying a person from synchronizing the authoritative state: a missed alert should not erase the underlying ride or bid.
chapters.prediction: Would assigning a phone a REST endpoint guarantee that a backend can reach it?
chapters.explanation: No. Address changes, NAT, firewalls and offline periods remain obstacles.
chapters.narration: A building maintenance app should alert a resident when a repair appointment changes. The scheduling server knows the resident's account, but that knowledge does not give it a reachable network endpoint on the resident's phone. The phone may change networks, sit behind address translation or have its application suspended. Treating the phone as an ordinary public HTTP server leaves those constraints unexplained, even if the notification payload is only a few bytes. Instead, the device or platform establishes an outbound delivery path that the backend can use indirectly. Now consider the phone being offline when the appointment changes twice. Decide whether to retain both changes, replace the first with the latest state, or simply notify the app to refresh. This is a product-level delivery policy, not a detail solved by opening a socket. Keep the authoritative appointment in durable storage so that reconnecting clients can recover their current state even when a notification never arrives.

chapters.title: Registration and mobile delivery
paragraphs: Mobile push services let an application backend address a registered app instance through platform infrastructure. The app obtains a provider-issued identifier and sends it to its authenticated backend. Later, the backend associates an event with the relevant installations and submits a notification. The operating system manages the delivery connection, avoiding a separate continuously active connection for every installed application.

Treat registration identifiers as changeable routing information rather than permanent user identities. A user can own multiple devices, and a device installation can receive a new identifier. Update registration records and remove invalid destinations. Provider acceptance is not proof of display or user attention; retention limits, connectivity and device policy affect delivery. Use notifications to prompt a state refresh when correctness matters.
chapters.prediction: A push provider accepts a request. Has the user necessarily seen it?
chapters.explanation: No. Acceptance, device receipt, application processing and human attention are separate milestones.
chapters.narration: A library app user signs in on a phone and a tablet. Each installation registers for platform notifications and sends its current provider-issued routing token to the authenticated backend. The backend associates both installations with the account. When a reserved book becomes ready, the notification service resolves the account to eligible installations and submits delivery requests. The account identifies the person; the tokens identify destinations through the platform's delivery mechanism. Now uninstall and reinstall the phone app. Its routing information may change, while the person's account remains the same. Registration updates and invalid-token cleanup are therefore part of normal operation. Logging out also requires a policy that prevents the next device user from receiving the previous user's private notifications. Provider acceptance only says a delivery request entered that provider's process; it does not prove the message was displayed or read. A notification can prompt a fresh authorized read of the library record instead of carrying all sensitive details itself.

chapters.title: WebSockets, long polling and alternatives
paragraphs: An active browser can open a WebSocket and exchange messages in both directions while the connection remains alive. Long polling instead leaves an HTTP request pending until data or a timeout arrives, then starts another request. Both permit an update to arrive without a fresh user action. Their latency and operational behavior differ from repeatedly making short periodic polling requests.

Choose transport from communication needs. Server-sent events provide a server-to-browser stream over HTTP; WebSockets support bidirectional messages. Browser background Web Push is a separate mechanism from an open page connection. Every active connection can break, so design reconnection, authentication renewal and recovery of missed state. A timeout such as sixty seconds is an implementation choice, not part of the definition of long polling.
chapters.prediction: Does a WebSocket by itself replay messages missed during a disconnected interval?
chapters.explanation: No. Replay or state resynchronization belongs to the application protocol.
chapters.narration: A workshop dashboard polls every ten seconds for a changed machine status. With changes occurring at arbitrary times, the average wait until the next poll is about five seconds, ignoring request latency. Reducing the interval lowers that wait but increases the number of requests even when nothing changes. A WebSocket keeps a bidirectional channel open, while long polling lets the server hold a request until data or a timeout becomes available. The connection does not eliminate state recovery. If a browser loses its network for thirty seconds, it may miss several transitions regardless of the chosen live transport. On reconnect, retrieve the current authoritative status or resume from a position supported by the application protocol. Distinguish a dashboard that needs only the latest temperature from an audit screen that needs every transition. That requirement determines how much history must be retained. Compare latency, idle connection resources and reconnect behaviour, rather than choosing a protocol solely because it is described as real time.

chapters.title: Routing to the correct connection
paragraphs: A distributed notification service must find the worker holding each live client connection. Other backend services should send a logical user notification rather than guess the physical socket owner. A registry connects user and installation identities to provider destinations or live connection identifiers. This allows the notification service to serve multiple devices and browser tabs without duplicating routing logic across domain services.

Connection records become stale when clients disconnect or workers fail. Remove obsolete entries, renew registrations and tolerate races between lookup and delivery. A managed gateway may expose a connection identifier rather than a raw socket address; the same lifecycle problem remains. Store durable business state separately so reconnecting clients can recover even when transient delivery fails, and authorize both subscription and outbound routing.
chapters.prediction: Steve has two browser tabs and one phone. Should the registry contain only one destination?
chapters.explanation: No. It needs the intended set of current destinations, with per-connection or per-installation lifecycle handling.
chapters.narration: An account has two browser tabs, one connected to notification worker A and another to worker B. An appointment service running elsewhere generates an update. Sending the update to an arbitrary notification worker is insufficient: only the worker holding a particular live connection can write to it. A registration directory maps the logical recipient to connection identifiers and their owners, allowing the notification layer to route to both tabs. Close one tab just after the directory lookup. The route can become stale between lookup and send, so lookup success cannot guarantee delivery. Clean up failed destinations and let reconnecting clients establish fresh registrations. Keep transport failures separate from the underlying appointment change, which remains stored independently. If the design promises recovery of missed updates, retain an appropriate event history or provide a fresh-state read. Trace a worker restart as well as a normal send; this reveals why connection ownership, authoritative data and notification progress are different kinds of state.

chapters.title: Choose what the architecture model must explain
paragraphs: An architectural model records selected design decisions, not every fact about the program. Components, connectors, interfaces, configurations and rationale answer different stakeholder questions. The web-system examples show how a cache, application, database, object store and external services can be placed in a shared picture. The important question is what each element and edge means and which decision the picture helps evaluate.

Choose detail and formality according to the benefit of creating and maintaining the model. Include constraints on interaction, concurrency or behavior when those constraints matter. Static structure and runtime state are different perspectives, although a running system can also change topology through scaling or redeployment. Functional and quality concerns can both be modeled; “prints medical records” leaves speed and confidentiality unresolved until the description specifies relevant conditions and evidence.
chapters.prediction: Is a more detailed model always more useful?
chapters.explanation: No. Detail incurs maintenance and cognitive costs; select what answers consequential stakeholder questions.
chapters.narration: Architecture modeling makes selected decisions explicit. Start with the question, then choose components, relationships, constraints and rationale that answer it. More detail is not automatically better. The model must remain understandable and maintainable, while preserving the assumptions needed to evaluate behavior and quality. Treat runtime state and structural organization as related but distinct perspectives.
chapters.focus: Choose what the architecture model must explain

chapters.title: Estimate before committing to implementation
paragraphs: Performance modeling can reveal a costly design before a full system exists. Execution graphs estimate scenario work; queueing networks estimate contention; other approaches can use simulation or learned relationships. Models allow early comparison of alternatives and resource needs, but their answers remain conditional on assumptions about operations, infrastructure and workload. A plausible model is an engineering aid rather than a performance guarantee.

Execution models in this unit omit resource contention. Their service costs therefore provide a baseline, not the response a busy production system must achieve. Finding an unacceptable baseline is valuable because queueing will not rescue it. Passing that check does not prove adequate loaded performance. Combine early models with prototypes and subsequent measurements, revising parameters as evidence becomes available instead of treating modeling and testing as mutually exclusive stages.
chapters.prediction: If an execution graph predicts 100 ms without contention, is 100 ms guaranteed under concurrent users?
chapters.explanation: No. Queueing, interference and model omissions can increase response time.
chapters.narration: Use early models to challenge a design while change is still affordable. An execution graph estimates required work without contention, making it useful for spotting obvious problems. A good baseline does not establish loaded performance. Refine assumptions with prototypes and measurements, then add queueing or simulation when competition for resources matters.

chapters.title: From execution cost to resource contention
paragraphs: A software execution model estimates the resources a scenario demands without competition from other requests. A queueing model adds that competition. A service station contains waiting work and one or more servers, where a server might represent a processor, disk or network link rather than a physical computer. Residence time includes both waiting and service; service time measures the resource work alone.

Kendall notation records assumptions about arrivals, service times, server count, capacity, population and scheduling. In the slide example, total capacity twenty includes three jobs in service and seventeen waiting. State this convention explicitly because “buffer” is ambiguous. Model choices matter: bursty arrivals, finite populations and priority scheduling can produce different behavior even when average service demand is unchanged. A useful model is precise about its boundary and assumptions.

chapters.title: Measure throughput and apply operational laws
paragraphs: An execution profile records arrivals, completions and busy intervals over a measurement period. For the supplied twenty-second observation, eight completions yield throughput 0.4 jobs per second and sixteen busy seconds yield utilization 0.8. Average service demand is two seconds per completed job under the accounting assumptions. These measurements describe different quantities; utilization is a fraction, throughput is a rate and residence time is a duration.

The utilization law connects throughput and service demand, U=X×S for a single service resource. Little’s law relates average jobs inside a boundary to throughput and average residence time, N=X×R. Use consistent boundaries and a stable observation regime; do not mix system throughput with a device queue length. The NFS exercise completes 10,800 requests in 1,800 seconds, giving six per second; three active requests imply average residence of half a second.

chapters.title: Understand single and multiple server queues
paragraphs: The M/M/1 model assumes Poisson arrivals, independent exponentially distributed service times and one server with an unbounded waiting room. In steady state it requires arrival rate λ below service rate μ. Its utilization is ρ=λ/μ, mean residence time is 1/(μ−λ), and mean jobs is ρ/(1−ρ). These expressions describe long-run averages under the model, not deterministic limits on individual requests.

Birth–death balance explains the geometric state distribution. At an empty system, departure rate is zero; at nonempty states it is μ. Multiple servers change departure capacity to min(n,m)μ and require a different waiting calculation such as Erlang C. Finite buffers change the model again: an infinite-queue tail probability is not automatically the exact blocking probability of a bounded system. Always define whether capacity includes the job being served.
