units.title: Secure Microservices: Boundaries, Tokens and Response
units.shortTitle: Secure Microservices: Boundaries, Tokens and Response
units.description: Protect service boundaries with verified identities, scoped access, isolation and incident response.

chapters.title: Protect the exposed service boundary
paragraphs: A microservice system has more communication paths and administrative surfaces than one isolated process. Begin by identifying which routes clients actually need. An API gateway can expose those routes, apply common checks and direct requests to internal services. Restricting direct access reduces opportunities to bypass those checks, but the gateway is one control rather than a reason to trust everything behind it.

Client application credentials and user identity answer different questions. A secret embedded in a distributed browser or mobile application cannot be assumed confidential. Apply request limits and protect the infrastructure control plane, while planning gateway capacity and failure behavior. Include outbound dependencies in the trust model: an internal service may call an external endpoint that supplies malicious data or receives sensitive information. Draw both directions of traffic before deciding where checks belong.
chapters.prediction: If only the gateway is publicly reachable, can an internal billing service skip authorization?
chapters.explanation: No. A compromised internal caller or a mistaken route can still reach it. Enforce resource permissions at a trustworthy boundary that cannot be bypassed.
chapters.narration: Start with the public boundary: expose only the routes clients need, apply common gateway protections and restrict management access. Then examine what happens after traffic enters the cluster. A gateway reduces exposure but does not make internal callers trustworthy. Distinguish a client application credential from the identity and permissions of the user behind a request.
chapters.focus: Walls/moat analogy, entry point, public/internal routes, application tokens, rate limits, management and outbound dependencies.

chapters.title: Verify peers and protect channels
paragraphs: Encryption is useful only when the connection reaches the intended peer. Certificate verification links a presented key to a trusted identity under the client’s policy. Accepting every certificate removes that assurance. A self-signed certificate can be deliberately trusted through an authenticated provisioning process; simply accepting any self-signed certificate does not establish the correct peer. Verification includes the intended service identity, not merely a recognizable issuer.

TLS protects data while it crosses the established channel. In mutual TLS, both sides authenticate with certificates; this identifies a workload or client credential, not automatically a human user or permission to perform every operation. Protect private keys and plan issuance, renewal and compromise response. Pinning narrows accepted credentials but adds rotation and recovery responsibilities. Keep authentication, confidentiality and application authorization distinct in the architecture diagram.
chapters.prediction: If a client encrypts traffic but accepts any certificate, has it authenticated the intended server?
chapters.explanation: No. It may establish an encrypted channel to an impostor; identity verification is essential.
chapters.narration: Follow the certificate trust decision before discussing encryption. The client must verify the intended service, not merely receive a certificate. Mutual TLS adds client-side credentials to the channel and can identify workloads. It still leaves application authorization to be decided. Key protection, certificate renewal and recovery are ongoing architectural responsibilities, especially when pinning is used.
chapters.focus: TLS handshake conceptual model, certificate trust, self-signed versus explicitly trusted, pinning, private keys and mTLS.

chapters.title: Contain compromise inside the cluster
paragraphs: An internal network should not imply unrestricted communication. List the connections each workload requires, then restrict both incoming and outgoing paths. Kubernetes namespaces organize resources but do not automatically isolate their network traffic. NetworkPolicy requires enforcement by the selected networking implementation. Separate intended policy from demonstrated behavior, and test whether an unrelated service can reach a protected dependency.

Outbound restrictions help reduce unwanted destinations and some SSRF consequences, but they complement rather than replace application validation. Runtime monitoring can report suspicious behavior; an alert is not necessarily a preventive control. Resource quotas bound aggregate namespace allocations, while workload requests and limits address individual resource behavior. These measures can reduce blast radius and resource contention without promising to eliminate denial of service. Define who investigates alerts and how a service is isolated without losing essential evidence.
chapters.prediction: Does placing billing and search in separate namespaces block search from contacting billing?
chapters.explanation: No. Namespaces alone do not impose that network boundary; enforced policies and the relevant selectors must establish it.
chapters.narration: Containment starts with a communication map. Allow required paths and consider outbound traffic as carefully as inbound traffic. Namespaces organize resources, while supported network policies enforce selected network boundaries. Monitoring and quotas add detection and resource controls. Evaluate each mechanism by the consequence it limits, and do not mistake an alert or configuration object for guaranteed prevention.
chapters.focus: Namespaces, ingress/egress, SSRF containment, Falco as runtime detection, quotas and denial-of-service limits.

chapters.title: Token trust, validation and revocation
paragraphs: A signed JWT carries claims plus a signature; its readable payload is not encrypted merely because it is signed. A service needs a validation policy: trusted issuer and keys, permitted algorithms, intended audience, token type and applicable time constraints. A valid signature alone does not establish that this token belongs at this API or that its subject may access the requested record.

Access and refresh tokens have different roles. Short access-token lifetimes limit exposure, while refresh-token rotation or sender constraints address renewal risk. Revoking a refresh token does not magically invalidate every already issued self-contained access token. Central issuance with local verification can reduce repeated authentication calls, but introduces key-distribution and revocation tradeoffs. OAuth concerns delegated authorization; OpenID Connect adds authentication conventions. Neither is synonymous with the JWT data format.
chapters.prediction: If a user’s refresh token is revoked, must a locally validated access token stop working immediately?
chapters.explanation: No. Immediate rejection requires an additional mechanism such as introspection or a revocation/version check; otherwise the access token may remain valid until expiry.
chapters.narration: Treat a token as a claim that must be evaluated in context. Verify its issuer, cryptographic protection, audience and time constraints, then authorize the operation. Follow access and refresh tokens separately through expiry and compromise. Central issuance and local verification offer a useful pattern, but revocation and key rotation must be explicit rather than assumed.
chapters.focus: JWT structure, access/refresh lifecycle, provider versus centralized/per-service issuance, asymmetric verification and internal/external identities.

chapters.title: Harden each service and its data paths
paragraphs: A service should expose only necessary interfaces and run with limited privileges. Non-root execution, reduced capabilities, a read-only filesystem where feasible and narrowly scoped workload credentials reduce consequences of compromise. Secrets should be managed with explicit access, rotation and revocation rather than hardcoded in source. Environment variables and mounted files each have exposure tradeoffs; a secret store still needs authentication and authorization.

Input handling must match the destination. Parameterized database operations separate data from SQL, contextual output encoding protects HTML contexts, and destination validation plus network controls help constrain outbound URL requests. An ORM can still execute unsafe raw queries. Error handling should avoid disclosing internal details while retaining useful protected diagnostics. Trust forwarded identity or IP information only from configured trusted intermediaries, and order middleware so identity and permission decisions occur before protected work.
chapters.prediction: Can a service trust X-Forwarded-For simply because the request contains that header?
chapters.explanation: No. Clients can supply headers. The trusted proxy path must overwrite or validate forwarded information, and network address still does not prove user permission.
chapters.narration: Apply security at the service as well as the perimeter. Reduce runtime privileges, expose only needed interfaces and manage secrets through their lifecycle. Validate data for its actual destination: SQL, HTML and outbound URLs require different controls. Shared middleware can make checks consistent, but its trust assumptions and execution order must be understood and tested.
chapters.focus: Ports, forwarded-header trust, error leakage, middleware, containers, SQL/RCE/XSS/SSRF defenses, deserialization and secret management.

chapters.title: Practice incident response with bounded simulations
paragraphs: The supplied Uber case distinguishes tabletop exercises, red-team operations and smaller repeatable simulations. These methods test different things: decision-making and escalation, broader adversary behavior, or focused detection and response. The historical example should not be treated as a statement of Uber’s current procedures. For this course, a tabletop preserves the architectural learning without running intrusion tools or accessing real credentials.

Assign roles for triage, service ownership, communications and decision authority. Introduce synthetic evidence in stages: suspicious token use, an unexpected outbound connection, then an unavailable dependency. Ask what evidence is needed, what can be contained and which users are affected. Record timing and assumptions, then conduct an after-action review with owners for improvements. Coverage mapped to ATT&CK techniques can reveal gaps, but a checked box does not prove that a control will detect every variation.
chapters.prediction: If a simulation triggers an alert, is the response process necessarily successful?
chapters.explanation: No. Someone must triage it, coordinate decisions, contain harm and recover; the exercise should test that complete chain.
chapters.narration: Use simulations to practice decisions as well as detections. Tabletop exercises, broad red-team engagements and focused repeatable tests answer different questions. Our course exercise stays with synthetic evidence and role-based discussion. Trace escalation, containment and recovery, then assign concrete improvements after the review. Coverage tracking is useful evidence, not a guarantee of future detection.
chapters.focus: Uber historical case; TTX/vSOC/CIRT/injects, red-team and atomic comparison, after-action review, coverage/ATT&CK; offensive execution details replaced by synthetic classroom evidence.

quiz.question: A gateway validates a JWT signature. Name two reasons a downstream grade service should still reject a request.
quiz.answer: The token may target a different audience or be expired, and the authenticated subject may lack permission for the specific grade record. Validate the relevant claims and enforce object-level authorization.

quiz.question: Separate namespaces and ResourceQuota objects exist. Does that prove traffic isolation and denial-of-service prevention?
quiz.answer: No. Network policies need supporting enforcement; quotas constrain aggregate allocations and do not stop all runtime exhaustion, request floods or dependency overload.

quiz.question: A service accepts an issuer’s valid signed JWT containing a readable email address. Does the signature make that claim confidential?
quiz.answer: No. Signing protects integrity and issuer authenticity under proper verification; confidentiality requires separate encryption and handling controls.

review.issue: Client secrets and rate limiting are described as universal gateway protections.
review.correction: Public clients cannot safely keep an embedded secret. Rate limiting mitigates some overload and abuse but does not guarantee denial-of-service prevention.

review.issue: TLS and mTLS are framed as one fixed handshake and authentication scheme.
review.correction: Use the conceptual model while noting protocol/cipher-mode differences. Verification must establish intended peer identity; mTLS authentication is distinct from application permission.

review.issue: Self-signed certificates are equated with no trust and pinning with unconditional safety.
review.correction: An explicitly provisioned trust anchor can be self-signed. Accept-all is unsafe; pinning needs deliberate rotation/recovery. Avoid presenting certificate validity as issuer signature alone.

review.issue: Each namespace is described as a network segment.
review.correction: Namespaces alone do not isolate traffic. NetworkPolicy needs a supporting plugin and correctly scoped ingress/egress rules.

review.issue: Egress rules and quotas are claimed to prevent software installation and denial of service.
review.correction: These reduce selected consequences, not all attacks. Quotas govern aggregate namespace resource consumption; combine them with appropriate workload and traffic controls.

review.issue: JWT always has three parts and signature guarantees trust.
review.correction: The three-part example is a compact signed JWS. JWTs may use other protections. Enforce an algorithm allowlist, trusted keys, issuer, audience and relevant claims; signed data is not automatically confidential.

review.issue: Refresh-token use automatically invalidates all compromised user tokens.
review.correction: Token rotation and revocation require explicit server mechanisms. Already issued local-verification access tokens can remain usable until expiry unless additional checks are designed.

review.issue: Not recommended label placement and asymmetric secret-key terminology are ambiguous.
review.correction: Call the issuer key private and verifier keys public. Central issuance with service-side verification is viable; do not condemn it based on ambiguous extracted layout. Clarify OAuth authorization versus OIDC authentication.

review.issue: Forwarded source IP is treated as trustworthy access-control input.
review.correction: Only trust forwarding information from a configured proxy chain that strips or overwrites untrusted values. IP allowlists complement, rather than establish, user/workload identity.

review.issue: One middleware order is presented as universal.
review.correction: Order depends on framework behavior and trust boundaries. Ensure identity exists before authorization, protected work follows checks, and exceptions do not expose secrets.

review.issue: ORMs, sanitization, read-only containers or lack of tools appear sufficient.
review.correction: Use parameter binding and context-specific encoding/validation. Raw ORM queries can remain unsafe. Runtime restrictions and secret-delivery mechanisms need complementary permission, rotation and revocation designs.

review.issue: Uber operations and the slide 50 execution chain may look like current procedures or a lab assignment.
review.correction: Label the case historical and turn it into a discussion-only exercise using synthetic evidence. No RAT execution, credential access, network scanning or exfiltration is part of this generated unit.

exercise.prompt: Draw a course-registration architecture with gateway, identity provider, enrollment service and billing service. State permitted network paths and which identity each hop verifies. Explain token validation and withdrawal of instructor privileges. Then run a paper tabletop: a synthetic alert reports a billing token used from an unexpected workload. Choose triage, containment, evidence and recovery steps; do not interact with live systems.
exercise.answer: Expose required gateway routes, restrict service/control-plane access and permit only needed ingress/egress. Verify workload identity on internal channels and user/token context at protected operations. Validate issuer, audience, signature and lifetime; enforce enrollment/billing permissions separately. State revocation latency for cached or self-contained tokens. In the tabletop preserve synthetic event records, confirm scope, isolate the affected credential/workload, rotate or revoke as appropriate, check dependent services, communicate impact and record owned improvements.

units.title: Case study: Uber’s real-time push platform
units.shortTitle: Case study: Uber’s real-time push platform
units.description: Study a historical push platform through delivery priorities, expiry and connection ownership.

chapters.title: From polling to separated responsibilities
paragraphs: The historical Uber case begins with rider and driver applications polling for changing trip state. The slides report that polling dominated gateway traffic and that startup requests competed on weak mobile networks. RAMEN separates the decision to send an update from creating its content and delivering it. This division targets both operational efficiency and the difficulty of migrating many existing features.

Fireball reacts to domain events and determines recipients and message types. The API gateway assembles payloads using domain services, reusing logic associated with earlier pull APIs. A delivery system then owns connections and retries. These are case-study responsibilities, not mandatory product names for every architecture. In a course system, enrolment events, timetable composition and device delivery can be separated in the same way.
chapters.prediction: Should the connection server also decide every business rule about when a ride update is needed?
chapters.explanation: Separating that decision reduces coupling between domain evolution and delivery infrastructure.
chapters.narration: The historical Uber case begins with rider and driver applications polling for changing trip state. The slides report that polling dominated gateway traffic and that startup requests competed on weak mobile networks. RAMEN separates the decision to send an update from creating its content and delivering it. This division targets both operational efficiency and the difficulty of migrating many existing features.
chapters.focus: Historical migration and separation of concerns

chapters.title: Priority, expiry and resumable delivery
paragraphs: RAMEN attaches delivery policy to payloads: priority determines which pending updates matter first, expiry limits how long an update remains useful, and replacement can retain the latest state instead of every intermediate version. The historical SSE protocol adds sequence numbers, reconnect cursors and separate acknowledgements. These application mechanisms supply recovery behavior that a persistent transport alone cannot guarantee to the user.

A lost acknowledgement is ambiguous: the client may have processed a message even though the server retries it. Consumers must therefore tolerate duplicates. Expiry also bounds the delivery promise: an offline device cannot receive a timely update indefinitely. Distinguish coalescing state snapshots from deduplicating identical messages; replacing an old location with a new location is reasonable, but dropping an independent payment event is different.
chapters.prediction: If the client processes sequence 3 but its acknowledgement is lost, may sequence 3 arrive again?
chapters.explanation: Yes. Retry can produce duplicates; the client needs safe repeat processing or message-ID tracking.
chapters.narration: RAMEN attaches delivery policy to payloads: priority determines which pending updates matter first, expiry limits how long an update remains useful, and replacement can retain the latest state instead of every intermediate version. The historical SSE protocol adds sequence numbers, reconnect cursors and separate acknowledgements. These application mechanisms supply recovery behavior that a persistent transport alone cannot guarantee to the user.
chapters.focus: Acknowledgements, retries and bounded retention

chapters.title: Scaling connection ownership
paragraphs: The slides describe an early RAMEN implementation using sharded connections and Redis, followed by a redesign separating connection handling, routing and cluster management. Treat the throughput and connection counts as reported historical observations. They illustrate why topology convergence and overloaded event loops can become important even when each individual message is small and the application’s business logic appears straightforward.

In the redesigned case, Streamgate handles protocol and storage work while a frontend routes requests to the appropriate worker. Helix and ZooKeeper manage topology-related responsibilities, and the cache and durable storage layers serve different purposes. The architectural lesson is ownership: changing a worker assignment must be coordinated with routing and recovery. More workers cannot help if clients or producers continue using stale ownership information.
chapters.prediction: Can doubling connection workers help if routing still sends all requests to the old owner?
chapters.explanation: Not reliably. Membership and routing convergence are part of the scaling design.
chapters.narration: The slides describe an early RAMEN implementation using sharded connections and Redis, followed by a redesign separating connection handling, routing and cluster management. Treat the throughput and connection counts as reported historical observations. They illustrate why topology convergence and overloaded event loops can become important even when each individual message is small and the application’s business logic appears straightforward.
chapters.focus: Topology, ownership and historical metrics

chapters.title: Protocol evolution and the reliability boundary
paragraphs: The case identifies long-tail delivery problems involving acknowledgement loss, inconsistent client behavior and limitations of the earlier unidirectional stream. Its later protocol work explores bidirectional communication and more standardized client support. Separate the enduring requirement from a particular transport choice: the service needs feedback about progress, recoverable state and a clear policy for clients whose networks disappear for extended periods.

Bidirectional streaming can carry acknowledgements promptly, but it does not turn a network failure into certainty about application effects. Define exactly what each acknowledgement means and which state survives a worker restart. The source’s reported server-side reliability is not an end-to-end guarantee that a person received or acted on an alert. Evaluate transport changes by measured recovery behavior and implementation consistency.
chapters.prediction: Does changing from SSE to a bidirectional RPC stream automatically create exactly-once application processing?
chapters.explanation: No. Durable state, acknowledgement meaning and duplicate handling still determine application effects.
chapters.narration: The case identifies long-tail delivery problems involving acknowledgement loss, inconsistent client behavior and limitations of the earlier unidirectional stream. Its later protocol work explores bidirectional communication and more standardized client support. Separate the enduring requirement from a particular transport choice: the service needs feedback about progress, recoverable state and a clear policy for clients whose networks disappear for extended periods.
chapters.focus: Transport evolution versus end-to-end guarantees

quiz.question: What are the three separated responsibilities in the RAMEN case?
quiz.answer: Deciding when/who to notify, composing the payload, and delivering it over client connections.

quiz.question: Why can replacing queued location updates save bandwidth?
quiz.answer: The latest location snapshot may supersede earlier snapshots, whereas independent business events generally cannot be discarded that way.

quiz.question: Why should historical server-side reliability not be read as human notification receipt?
quiz.answer: It measures a particular server boundary; device connectivity, application processing and user attention are separate.

review.issue: Historical scale and reliability numbers could appear current.
review.correction: Attribute them to the historical engineering case; do not claim they describe Uber today.

review.issue: At-least-once phrasing hides TTL and acknowledgement ambiguity.
review.correction: Explain duplicates after lost acknowledgements and retry only within retention/expiry assumptions.

review.issue: gRPC implies automatic QUIC interoperability.
review.correction: Teach bidirectional gRPC streaming; do not equate ordinary gRPC deployments with QUIC transport support without implementation-specific evidence. Standard gRPC documentation describes HTTP/2-based transport.

exercise.prompt: Adapt RAMEN responsibilities to a course waitlist. Which updates can be replaced and which require durable handling?
exercise.answer: An event trigger identifies affected students; a composition layer builds the current offer; delivery tracks destinations and acknowledgements. A refreshed queue-position snapshot can replace an older one; a seat offer with expiry needs durable state, explicit acceptance and safe retries.

units.title: Architecture styles and their tradeoffs
units.description: Compare repositories, pipelines, layers, interpreters, control loops and peer-to-peer systems.

chapters.title: Describe a style through its constraints
paragraphs: An architectural style defines a vocabulary of components and connectors together with constraints on their organization and behavior. A label such as layered or client–server is therefore only the beginning of a description. Identify what components do, what communication means and which arrangements are permitted. The same graph shape can represent different styles if its edges have different semantics.

The opening examples combine several ideas: distributed communication, objects, layers and pipelines. Real systems can combine styles, so classification should clarify a design rather than force an exclusive label. Ask what problem a style addresses, which invariants must hold and what advantages require those invariants. The slide list includes implicit invocation but does not develop a dedicated treatment; event-driven content elsewhere can supply that connection without implying it is fully covered here.
chapters.prediction: Can one system use both repository and pipeline structures?
chapters.explanation: Yes. Different responsibilities or views may combine styles; explain where each applies and how their constraints interact.
chapters.narration: Describe architectural styles using components, connectors and constraints. A name alone does not explain behavior or tradeoffs. Real systems often combine styles, so identify which part of the system each description fits. Evaluate the assumptions that make an advantage possible, and use shared vocabulary to make decisions easier to inspect rather than to assign labels.
chapters.focus: Describe a style through its constraints

chapters.title: Repository and blackboard architectures
paragraphs: A repository architecture centers collaboration on a shared body of information. Independent components read or modify that state according to a common schema. An IDE offers a useful example because multiple tools can inspect and transform program information. A blackboard specialization allows cooperating computations to contribute partial results that other computations use, with coordination organized around the evolving shared information.

Centralized data management can consolidate access policy, backup and concurrency control. It also creates coupling through the data model: a schema change can affect many consumers even when their code does not call one another. Persistence and distribution are implementation choices, not automatic consequences of drawing one repository box. Ask who owns schema evolution, how concurrent updates are coordinated and whether the repository becomes a capacity or availability constraint.
chapters.prediction: If repository clients never call each other, are they independent of each other’s changes?
chapters.explanation: Not completely. They share schema and data semantics, so changes can affect other clients through the repository.
chapters.narration: The repository style coordinates components through shared information. It can simplify data management while coupling clients to a common model. Blackboard systems extend the idea through cooperating computations. Examine schema ownership, concurrency and failure behavior before claiming easy reuse or centralized control; one shared box does not automatically provide scalable or highly available storage.
chapters.focus: Repository and blackboard architectures

chapters.title: Pipes, filters and compiler hybrids
paragraphs: Filters transform streams and pipes carry output to subsequent input. In the pure style, filters avoid shared state and do not depend on the identity of adjacent filters. Compatible data contracts let stages be replaced or reordered when semantics allow. A pipeline is a linear specialization; batch sequential processing waits for an entire input batch before the next transformation produces its result.

The shell example illustrates composition, while the compiler history shows why pure categories can be insufficient. Compiler phases may follow an ordered pipeline while sharing symbol tables or an intermediate representation, forming a hybrid with repository structure. Streaming can support overlap, but throughput, buffering and synchronization still matter. Data conversion between stages introduces cost, and interactive feedback may require additional coordination beyond a one-way transformational flow.
chapters.prediction: If compiler phases all update a shared symbol table, is the design a pure stateless pipe-and-filter system?
chapters.explanation: No. It combines pipeline sequencing with shared repository state.
chapters.narration: Pipes and filters compose transformations through data contracts. A linear pipeline is one specialization, and batch processing changes when output becomes available. Compiler examples show that practical systems often add shared representations, creating hybrids. Consider conversion cost, buffering and feedback before assuming that connecting reusable stages automatically gives good performance or supports every interaction pattern.
chapters.focus: Pipes, filters and compiler hybrids

chapters.title: Objects and layers as boundaries
paragraphs: Object-oriented organization groups state with operations that preserve its invariants. Clients should rely on a contract rather than internal representation. Shared mutable objects can still create unexpected interactions when one client changes state another observes. Encapsulation reduces certain dependencies, but does not make every implementation change invisible or require hard-coded identities in every caller; indirection can manage references.

Layering organizes services by abstraction and restricts dependencies between them. Strict layering normally permits adjacent interactions; relaxed designs document deliberate bypasses. A layer is logical organization, while a tier describes deployment separation, so several layers may reside in one process or tier. Stable contracts can localize changes, but effects may propagate when behavior or assumptions change. Evaluate dependency direction and runtime cost instead of assuming a fixed upper bound on affected layers.
chapters.prediction: Does a three-layer codebase require three physical servers?
chapters.explanation: No. Layers express logical responsibility; deployment tiers and server count are separate choices.
chapters.narration: Objects encapsulate state and contracts; layers organize services by abstraction. Both help manage dependencies but do not erase behavioral coupling. Distinguish logical layers from physical deployment tiers. Shared mutable state and changes in interface meaning can still propagate, so evaluate the actual contracts and dependency rules rather than assuming isolation from the diagram alone.
chapters.focus: Objects and layers as boundaries

chapters.title: Interpreter and virtual-machine architectures
paragraphs: An interpreter architecture represents a program as data and uses an execution engine to advance it. The model distinguishes the interpreted program, its state and the engine’s state. This separation can make an unavailable machine or language executable on an existing platform. It also introduces responsibility for instruction semantics, validation and runtime behavior that ordinary direct execution may not expose in the same way.

Virtual machines need not be implemented solely through interpretation. The JVM specification defines an abstract machine without requiring a particular implementation technique; compilation and hybrid execution are possible. The deck’s Java and compiler-bootstrap examples connect runtime organization to build-time architecture. Portability depends on the specified abstraction and compatible implementations, while performance depends on execution strategy and workload. Treat specific implementation-version statements as historical examples unless they have been rechecked.
chapters.prediction: Does running JVM bytecode imply that every instruction is interpreted one at a time?
chapters.explanation: No. The specification permits different implementation technologies, including compilation.
chapters.narration: Interpreter architectures make a program and its execution state explicit data managed by an engine. This can support portability or simulate a machine that is not directly available. A virtual machine is an abstraction, not a requirement to interpret every instruction. Consider compilation, validation and build-time dependencies when explaining the complete execution architecture.
chapters.focus: Interpreter and virtual-machine architectures

chapters.title: Control systems and feedback
paragraphs: A process-control architecture aims to keep a controlled variable near a desired set point. Sensors measure relevant variables, and a controller chooses changes to manipulated variables. Cruise control provides a concrete vocabulary: desired speed is the set point, measured speed is feedback and throttle is manipulated. These roles describe the causal relationship, not merely a chain of function calls.

Feedback adjusts actions using observed results; open-loop control does not use the controlled output to correct its action. An open-loop approach may be adequate under predictable conditions, while disturbances make feedback valuable. A software architecture must also consider measurement delay, failure and actuator limits, even if a simple block diagram omits them. Preserve the distinction between an explanatory teaching model and a design validated for a safety-critical application.
chapters.prediction: If a heater follows a fixed schedule without measuring temperature, is it closed-loop temperature control?
chapters.explanation: No. Without feedback from the controlled variable, it is open loop for temperature.
chapters.narration: Process-control architecture separates the process, measurements and control decisions. Identify the controlled variable, manipulated variable and set point. Feedback uses observed results to adjust action; open-loop control does not. Simple diagrams explain these relationships, but an implemented controller must also address timing, disturbances and limits before its behavior can be judged reliable.
chapters.focus: Control systems and feedback

chapters.title: Client–server responsibilities and remote calls
paragraphs: Client–server organization gives one component a requesting role and another a service-providing role in an interaction. A file server supplies files, while a database server can execute queries near the stored data and return selected results. Remote communication makes message meaning, latency, availability and discovery part of the design. One component may act as server for one interaction and client for another.

Centralizing a service can simplify management and allow heterogeneous clients, but horizontal scaling depends on state, coordination and routing. Query processing at the server may reduce transfer for selective queries; it does not guarantee small responses for every workload. Location transparency can simplify interfaces without removing network failure. Explain timeout, retry and authorization responsibilities alongside the boxes so the design remains meaningful when a service is slow or unavailable.
chapters.prediction: Is a remote database query equivalent to a local procedure call in its failure behavior?
chapters.explanation: No. Communication failures and ambiguous outcomes require explicit timeout, retry and consistency reasoning.
chapters.narration: Client–server describes roles in an interaction. Keeping query processing near data can reduce some transfers, but network and failure behavior remain architectural concerns. Discovery, state and coordination affect scaling. A useful diagram explains who requests what and how the interaction behaves when the service is slow, unavailable or returns an uncertain outcome.
chapters.focus: Client–server responsibilities and remote calls

chapters.title: Peer-to-peer structure and practical hybrids
paragraphs: Peer-to-peer systems distribute service roles among participants rather than assigning all work to one permanent server. Peers can both request and provide data, and the overlay need not connect everyone directly. BitTorrent distributes pieces among participants, allowing downloaders to contribute verified pieces before completing the entire file. A complete participant can continue serving as a seed, but partial participation is already useful.

Decentralized data transfer does not imply the absence of centralized discovery or bootstrap dependencies. The source’s original Napster characterization should be treated as a hybrid example rather than a proof of fully decentralized control. Availability and privacy depend on the actual protocol, peer behavior and metadata exposure. Networks can partition, peers can disappear and discovery can fail, so assess resilience from concrete replication and routing mechanisms rather than from the peer-to-peer label alone.
chapters.prediction: Must a BitTorrent participant finish the entire file before uploading useful data?
chapters.explanation: No. The protocol allows peers to exchange available pieces while downloads are still in progress.
chapters.narration: Peer-to-peer systems let participants share both client and server roles. BitTorrent gains capacity from exchanging pieces during download, not only after completion. Check discovery and bootstrap mechanisms before claiming full decentralization. Resilience, privacy and scaling depend on the protocol and peer behavior, including partitions and unavailable or untrustworthy participants. Keep the model boundary explicit and connect each conclusion to its assumptions.
chapters.focus: Peer-to-peer structure and practical hybrids

quiz.question: What distinguishes a layer from a tier?
quiz.answer: A layer organizes logical functionality or abstraction; a tier describes deployment separation.

quiz.question: Why is a compiler with shared intermediate representation a hybrid?
quiz.answer: Its passes may form a pipeline while sharing repository state, so it does not satisfy pure independent-filter assumptions.

quiz.question: Does peer-to-peer imply no single point of failure?
quiz.answer: No. Discovery, bootstrap, identity or scarce data replicas may remain centralized or fragile.

review.issue: Terminology claim is historical; implicit invocation is listed but not developed.
review.correction: Present styles as a useful vocabulary with varying definitions. Cross-link event-driven units for implicit invocation rather than claiming this deck fully teaches it.

review.issue: Claims that all callers must change with identity or that at most two layers change are too absolute.
review.correction: Indirection can manage identities; preserved contracts can localize changes, while behavioral changes can propagate across multiple layers.

review.issue: JVM presented as inherently interpreted; Emacs version note can date.
review.correction: A JVM is not inherently interpreted; the specification permits compilation and other implementations. Keep Emacs 28 as a historical example or omit the version claim.

review.issue: BitTorrent seeding wording may imply upload starts only after completion.
review.correction: Peers exchange available pieces during download; seed denotes a peer with the complete content.

review.issue: Original Napster called serverless; peer-to-peer advantages presented as guarantees.
review.correction: Original Napster used centralized discovery/indexing; treat it as hybrid. Do not promise privacy, availability or elimination of all single points of failure without inspecting discovery and data distribution. The court opinion documents its server-side collective directory.

review.issue: Unexpected swarm robotics slide retains unrelated database-server text.
review.correction: Remove the duplicated database description and use the robotics example only if its communication/control mechanism is explained from a verified source.

review.issue: Many figures are diagram-only in extraction.
review.correction: All extracted text reviewed. Figure geometry, edge labels and missing images were not visually validated; examples are explained only to the extent supported by available text.

exercise.prompt: Choose a style or hybrid for an IDE, a log transformation job and a room-temperature controller. State one invariant and one risk for each.
exercise.answer: IDE: repository-centered tools share a program model; schema evolution couples clients. Log job: pipes and filters agree on record format and avoid shared state; buffering and conversion can bottleneck. Temperature controller: feedback adjusts output from measured temperature; delayed or faulty sensing can undermine control.

units.title: Asynchronous processing and message queues
units.description: Separate acceptance from completion and design queue-based work for retries and backpressure.

chapters.title: Accepted is different from completed
paragraphs: A synchronous request returns after the promised operation finishes; an asynchronous request can return once the system accepts responsibility for later work. Both can use HTTP. The important distinction is the contract, not whether a response exists. Sending an email, preparing a large download or provisioning a virtual machine can return an operation identifier while the requested work continues elsewhere.

Clients that need an outcome can poll an operation record, receive an authenticated callback or use another notification channel. Define pending, running, successful and failed states and explain retention. A webhook needs an accessible endpoint and its own retry policy. A user-facing acknowledgement should say accepted when completion is still uncertain; operational logs alone are rarely sufficient feedback for a consequential user action.
chapters.prediction: Does an immediate successful HTTP response prove the email reached its recipient?
chapters.explanation: Only if the API explicitly promises that milestone; an asynchronous acceptance usually does not.
chapters.narration: A researcher requests an export of a large experiment dataset. Waiting for every file to be prepared inside the initial request could exceed a useful response deadline. Instead, the service validates the request, records an export job and returns a job identifier. That response means the service accepted responsibility for attempting the export. It does not mean a downloadable archive already exists, so the user interface should display queued or processing rather than completed. The client can later query the job record for success or a failure reason. A webhook is another option for a client with a reachable endpoint, but it introduces its own authentication and retry contract. A phone behind a changing network cannot simply be assumed to accept callbacks. Include a terminal failure state so that accepted jobs do not appear pending forever. Trace a worker failure after acceptance and identify how another worker discovers the job. The shorter response time moves completion tracking into explicit application state.
chapters.focus: Make acceptance and completion separate observable states

chapters.title: Queues as durable work contracts
paragraphs: A queue lets a producer describe work and hand it to consumers that run later. The message schema is an interface contract, including identifiers, required fields and version behavior. In the tweet example, one service accepts publication work, another expands it into feed updates, and another handles optional notifications. This separates stages with different cost, latency and failure requirements.

Acknowledge consumer work after the intended durable effect, then plan for crashes between effect and acknowledgement. Retried work may repeat, so use idempotency keys or transactional coordination where required. Durable acceptance also depends on how publication reaches the queue; changing a database and publishing separately creates a failure gap. A transactional outbox is one design for recording the event alongside the business change.

chapters.narration: A document service places a preview-generation request on a queue. The message contains a job identifier, document identifier, desired representation and schema version. These fields are an API contract even though no synchronous response carries the finished preview. The worker must know which document version to process and where to record the result. A queue containing only an ambiguous instruction such as generate preview leaves important business decisions to guesswork. Consider a worker that stores the preview and crashes before acknowledging the message. Redelivery may cause the same job to run again. Use the stable job identifier and a suitable result-update rule so that repetition does not create conflicting visible outcomes. Acknowledgement timing should reflect the actual persistence boundary, not merely receipt into memory. Likewise, an in-process queue lost during a restart provides a different contract from durable broker storage. The architecture should state what survives each failure and which component owns recovery, rather than treating every queue icon as equivalent.

chapters.title: Independent scaling and queue boundaries
paragraphs: Queues distribute pending work across consumers and smooth a temporary mismatch between arrival and processing rates. Producers and consumers can scale independently, but the broker has its own capacity and durability limits. An in-process queue is simple but may vanish with the process. A separate broker or replicated service provides different persistence and recovery options, with additional operational cost and coordination.

Pull-based and push-based delivery affect connection management rather than determining business correctness. Retained logs differ from destructive work queues: a log keeps records for replay, and consumers track progress. Kafka illustrates partitioned logs, although the slides’ ZooKeeper discussion is historical. Select retention, consumer grouping and acknowledgement semantics deliberately instead of assuming all products listed as queues behave identically under load or failure.

Two workers can process ten jobs per second, so the backlog grows by approximately ten jobs each second during that burst. Adding two more workers could match the arrival rate if shared storage and other dependencies have spare capacity. The queue exposes the difference between accepting work and providing enough capacity to finish it. Keep admission through the service API, where authorization, validation and workload limits belong, rather than letting public clients publish arbitrary broker messages. Producers and consumers can scale separately, but the queue itself and downstream storage still have limits. A larger queue changes how long work can wait; it does not increase processing throughput. chapters.title: Backpressure, ordering and recovery
paragraphs: A bounded queue must eventually reject, delay or otherwise regulate producers when it cannot safely accept more work. This backpressure is a protective control rather than merely an error to hide. Monitor oldest-message age as well as depth, because a small queue of expensive jobs can still violate latency goals. Retry policies should use limits and backoff instead of continuously recycling failures.

Ordering is scoped to the chosen system and partitioning design. Many brokers offer useful per-key or per-partition order, but concurrent consumers and retries complicate observed completion order. Group related work by key or use sequence checks when order matters; merging everything into one giant message is not the only solution. Keep public clients behind an authenticated application boundary unless the messaging service explicitly supports that access model.
chapters.prediction: Can a globally distributed workload still preserve order for each individual account?
chapters.explanation: Yes, for example through account-key partitioning and ordered processing, while allowing different accounts to proceed independently.
chapters.narration: Suppose a report queue holds six hundred pending jobs and its workers finish ten jobs per second while new arrivals temporarily stop. A rough drain time is sixty seconds. If arrivals continue at eight jobs per second, the net drain rate is only two, stretching the estimate to five minutes. These simplified calculations explain why queue length alone is insufficient: arrival rate, service rate and the age of waiting work determine user experience. Set an admission policy before storage fills. Depending on the product, reject excess work, postpone low-priority jobs or coalesce requests that genuinely supersede one another. Recovery also needs ordering rules. Two changes to the same report configuration should not accidentally apply in reverse order merely because different workers finish at different times. A broker's guarantees depend on its configuration and partitioning, so define the scope of required order. Bounded retries and a visible failed-job state prevent one malformed message from consuming capacity indefinitely while legitimate work waits.

chapters.title: From direct calls to implicit invocation
paragraphs: With a direct call, the caller names the operation it wants another component to perform. With implicit invocation, a component announces an event and registered handlers react. A debugger can announce that execution stopped, letting an editor highlight source without the debugger depending on that editor’s implementation. The same idea supports user-interface observers and database triggers inside a single application.

The connector determines dispatch semantics. An in-process event can invoke handlers synchronously, while a distributed event bus often delivers asynchronously. A publisher should not assume which subscribers exist or that they finish in a particular order unless the contract explicitly provides it. This enables extension and replacement, but makes the full chain of effects harder to see during debugging and error handling.
chapters.prediction: Must every implicit event invocation cross a network or run asynchronously?
chapters.explanation: No. A local connector can invoke handlers synchronously; distributed messaging is one specialization.

chapters.title: Event-driven architecture and brokered fan-out
paragraphs: An event describes something that happened, such as a seat becoming available. Consumers can react independently: notify a student, update a dashboard or record an audit trail. A publisher-subscriber intermediary routes events to interested subscriptions, reducing the producer’s need to track every consumer address. Topics and filters let consumers select relevant changes without requiring a new direct integration for each interested service.

Decoupling does not erase contracts. Event fields, identifiers, versions and authorization rules remain shared responsibilities. Separate subscriptions can maintain their own progress, while competing workers within one subscription may share its load. Request/reply communication needs correlation identifiers and an explicit reply path when a caller requires a specific result. Choose that pattern deliberately rather than hiding a mandatory synchronous dependency behind an event.
chapters.prediction: If analytics and notifications both need each enrolment event, should they compete for a single work item?
chapters.explanation: No. They need independent subscriptions or equivalent fan-out so each receives the event stream.
chapters.narration: A laboratory announces that an experiment has finished. The reporting service needs the result for a summary, and an audit service needs it for its own record. If both merely compete to remove one message from the same work queue, only one may receive each event. Independent reactions require separate subscription progress or an equivalent fan-out arrangement. Within the reporting subscription, multiple workers can share processing responsibility without changing the audit service's progress. The message still needs an explicit contract: experiment identifier, event identifier, schema version and enough context to retrieve or interpret the result. A broker can route messages, but cannot decide whether the reporting service needs a snapshot of the old result or may read its latest state. Draw the two subscriptions separately and fail one consumer. Explain which backlog grows and whether the other continues. This exercise connects asynchronous queue mechanisms to event-driven structure while keeping the distinction between an instruction to one worker and a fact announced to several consumers.

chapters.title: Delivery, ordering and poison messages
paragraphs: Subscribers must plan for duplicates, failures and delayed delivery. An idempotent handler prevents repeated execution from creating an extra effect, but it does not make out-of-order changes safe. Include entity versions or process related events in an ordered partition when sequence matters. A priority queue changes which message runs first; it is not a substitute for preserving business-event order.

Repeatedly failing messages need bounded retries and a dead-letter workflow with diagnosis and controlled replay. Expiry prevents obsolete work from consuming resources, while scheduled availability postpones otherwise valid work. Monitor each subscription’s lag so one slow consumer is visible without blocking all others. Eventual consistency is an application choice with limits, especially when a stale view can authorize an irreversible action.
chapters.prediction: Does making a handler idempotent guarantee that version 4 cannot overwrite version 5?
chapters.explanation: No. Duplicate safety and ordering are different; compare versions or enforce the required sequence.
chapters.narration: A subscriber records an experiment-completed event and then sends a researcher a notification. If it crashes after sending but before recording progress, a retry can send the notification again. Repeated delivery and repeated business effects are different issues: a stable event identifier lets the handler recognize a prior effect only when the relevant state is recorded with an appropriate consistency rule. Simply labelling the handler idempotent does not establish that rule. Now deliver result version three before version two. Duplicate detection alone cannot prevent an old version from overwriting a newer result. Define ordering per experiment or reject obsolete updates using their version. When a malformed event repeatedly fails, bound retries and retain enough information for diagnosis and controlled replay. Monitor subscription age as well as message counts so a small set of stuck events is visible. These decisions belong to the consumer contract and broker configuration; a distributed delivery system does not offer one universal ordering or exactly-once guarantee for every downstream effect.

chapters.title: ROS as an architectural example

Do not transfer every topology assumption across versions. A robot also requires deliberate delivery and timing policies: a fresh camera frame and an emergency stop do not have identical needs. Pub/sub modularity helps composition but does not establish safety by itself.

chapters.title: Distributed aggregates and data movement
paragraphs: Serving independent requests is different from calculating one answer over a large shared dataset. For a global maximum, each worker can compute a local maximum and send one candidate to a coordinator. The coordinator takes the maximum of those candidates, so little data moves. Other operations need richer summaries or repeated communication, making network cost part of algorithm design rather than an incidental implementation detail.

For a mean, combine sums and counts instead of averaging unequal-sized partitions’ means. Exact median selection is more involved: a pivot-based algorithm counts values below, equal to and above the pivot and narrows the target rank. Duplicates and even-sized inputs require explicit treatment. Hardware bandwidth examples provide lower bounds only under stated assumptions; use decimal petabytes consistently or label binary units correctly.
chapters.prediction: Can we average each month’s average order value to obtain the overall average?
chapters.explanation: Only when counts are equal. In general combine total sums and counts.
chapters.narration: A sensor analysis job estimates the average reading across two partitions. One holds ten readings averaging twenty, and the other holds ninety readings averaging forty. Averaging the two local averages gives thirty, but the correct global mean is thirty-eight. Each worker must return both a sum and a count: two hundred plus three thousand six hundred, divided by one hundred. The summary must preserve the information needed to combine unequal partitions correctly. Compare that with finding the global minimum: each worker needs to send only its local minimum. The amount and meaning of intermediate data depend on the operation. Sending all raw readings to one coordinator may be correct, but can destroy the benefit of distributing the work. Design the summary, estimate transfer volume and then identify where combination happens. Some calculations require multiple communication rounds or richer intermediate state. More workers reduce only the parallel portion of the cost; data movement and coordination still need an explicit place in the performance model.

chapters.title: MapReduce and finite batch jobs
paragraphs: MapReduce asks a programmer to transform input records into intermediate key-value pairs, then combine values sharing a key. For word counting, the mapper emits one pair per word occurrence and the reducer sums counts for each word. The shuffle groups intermediate data by key. Scheduling, distribution and retries belong largely to the framework, so the program can focus on the transformations.

A batch job works on a bounded input and eventually finishes; it does not imply sequential execution. Multiple tasks can run in parallel, and several jobs can be chained through intermediate results. Data locality can reduce traffic, but shuffle still transfers information among workers. A skewed key can overload a reducer, and retried tasks mean side effects outside the framework need careful design.
chapters.prediction: What happens if the mapper returns immediately on the first word inside its loop?
chapters.explanation: It counts only the first word; it must emit or accumulate a pair for every occurrence.
chapters.narration: A transport agency wants total delay minutes by route from a finite day of trip records. Each mapper emits the route identifier and that trip's delay. The shuffle groups values by route, and each reducer sums its group. The programmer specifies meaningful transformations while the framework arranges tasks and intermediate movement. Following one route through those stages makes the key's role concrete: it determines which records must meet for aggregation. If one route has most of the trips, its reducer may dominate completion time even when other reducers finish early. Local combining can reduce transfer for a sum, but the design still needs to account for skew and recovery. A framework that retains reusable intermediate datasets in memory can help repeated analyses, while its lineage or persistence rules determine recovery after lost state. These are bounded batch computations. They do not by themselves specify event-time windows or handling of an endless stream, so keep those separate requirements visible when comparing batch and streaming architectures.

chapters.title: Continuous streams and state
paragraphs: Stream processing reacts to an ongoing sequence rather than waiting for a complete dataset. Monitoring and recommendations may benefit from short update latency, while historical reporting can tolerate larger batch intervals. Low latency is a target, not an automatic guarantee. A stream operator may still wait for enough evidence, and overloaded consumers can accumulate lag even when the architecture is called real time.

Stateful stream computations need rules for windows, late arrivals, duplicates and recovery. Distinguish event time from the time a processor receives the event. The slides introduce Storm through sources and processing components; treat ease-of-operation and feature comparisons as contextual rather than universal. Compare batch and streaming on freshness, boundedness and operational requirements, not on the assumption that one handles large data and the other does not.

chapters.title: The thread-pool Leader/Followers pattern
paragraphs: The Leader/Followers concurrency pattern coordinates a pool of threads waiting for events. One thread leads by waiting on an event source; when an event arrives, another follower can become leader while the previous leader handles the work. The purpose is efficient event dispatch with controlled coordination overhead, not replication of durable data across a cluster of machines.

Correct handoff protects shared event sources and avoids having every thread compete for the same notification. Benefits depend on workload and runtime, and a blocked handler still needs appropriate timeout or cancellation behavior. Do not import distributed consensus claims into this thread-pool pattern: a new leading thread is not equivalent to safely electing a database leader after a network partition. Distinguish the two before discussing fault tolerance.
chapters.prediction: Does promoting another waiting thread provide replicated durability after machine failure?
chapters.explanation: No. Thread leadership manages local concurrency; durable distributed recovery is a separate design.

chapters.title: Kafka partition leaders and replicated logs
paragraphs: Kafka illustrates a different use of leader and follower terminology. A partition has a leader responsible for its log operations and replica followers that copy its data. Leadership can move after failure under a cluster coordination policy. Several partitions can distribute leadership across brokers, so one leader per partition does not mean the entire system has only one active writer.

Durability and availability depend on acknowledgements, in-sync replicas and election policy; replication alone is not an unconditional guarantee. A lagging replica may be unsuitable for safe promotion. The slides’ ZooKeeper control-plane account is historical, while Kafka 4 uses KRaft. For the e-commerce analytics example, distinguish ingestion durability from successful downstream computation and from committing external business effects exactly once.
